EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:21:56 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 French school protests to continue, after prime minister ignores demands https://euobserver.com/241687/french-school-protests-to-continue-after-prime-minister-ignores-demands/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:21:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241687 Two-weeks long protests by French high-school students demanding better education conditions risk getting more heated due the French government's lack of response.]]> Two-weeks long protests by French high-school students demanding better education conditions risk getting more heated due the French government’s lack of response.

For his part, French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu told parliament on Wednesday (7 October) the first proposals on education reform would be published at the end of the month.

He spoke after 250,000 demonstrators took to the streets across the country on Tuesday (6 October), according to interior ministry fiigures.

But the High School Student Union (Union Syndicaire Lycéenne, USL) said the number was as high as 450,000, including solidarity protests in most universities.

Pupils, joined by parents, teachers, and labour unions, want an end to teacher shortages and urgent renovations of run-down school buildings.

“Today, the balance of power is in our favour,” said Marius Mesnil, the USL’s co-general secretary, on Monday. 

The secondary school teachers’ union (Syndicat National des Enseignements de Secondaire, SNES) also called Lecornu’s inaction “unacceptable.”

Some 715 police officers, 215 students and 85 school staff members have been injured during the protests, with 18 internal probes were launched to investigate police brutality since 21 September, when the movement first erupted, after being sparked by a teachers’ protest.

A school in Nantes, in the west of the country, was set on fire, and protesters regularly light trash bins and make barricades in city centres.

The minister of interior has suspended the use of stun grenades after a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off in a violent confrontation with police on Monday.

]]> EU disowns Vilnius event that warned of US political interference, but France maintains support https://euobserver.com/241678/eu-disowns-vilnius-event-that-warned-of-us-political-interference-but-france-maintains-support/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:13:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241678 US pressure pushed some European governments to disown a Vilnius conference on disinformation and interference, which had dared to ask if America itself was now warping European politics.]]> An annual conference on foreign information manipulation opened in Vilnius this week with a sensitive question on its agenda: Can the United States be considered a threat to Europe’s information space?

And the question caused a diplomatic incident.

EU DisinfoLab’s annual #Disinfo2026 conference, held in Vilnius on 7 and 8 October, brings together researchers, journalists, civil society groups, technology specialists and policymakers working on “foreign information manipulation and interference”, known as FIMI in EU jargon.

The programme was to look at moving beyond analysis of disinformation to practical responses, including disruption, deterrence, and litigation. 

But shortly before the conference several of its government supporters withdrew their official backing.

The Lithuanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Global Affairs Canada (GAC), and the European External Action Service (EEAS) all disappeared from the conference’s list of sponsors.

The dispute centred on a panel entitled “USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back”.

According to the published programme, the session asked how the European counter-disinformation community could build resilience without Washington and what solidarity should look like in a fractured transatlantic relationship. 

Reuters reported that the US State Department had lobbied Canada and European allies over their support for the conference.

Three US officials familiar with the matter and correspondence reviewed said American officials had contacted counterparts in Lithuania, Canada and France.

And the US diplomats persuaded the Canadian and Lithuanian foreign ministries to distance themselves.

]]> Morocco’s surveillance state does not stop at Western Sahara — and Europe can no longer pretend not to know https://euobserver.com/241454/moroccos-surveillance-state-does-not-stop-at-western-sahara-and-europe-can-no-longer-pretend-not-to-know/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:50:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241454 As new evidence emerges of Moroccan spying on Sahrawi activists, including in Europe, European governments continue to deepen their security ties with Rabat without seriously questioning how those capabilities are being used.]]> In April 2021, I told The Guardian that Sahrawi activists were having their phones and internet connections hacked.

At the time, we could describe what was happening to us. We could not see the machinery behind it.

Five years later, Amnesty International’s new investigation, “We Start With the Verdict”: Inside Morocco’s Surveillance Machine, gives those warnings a disturbing new context.

Amnesty describes a surveillance ecosystem involving spyware, physical surveillance, location tracking, informants, judicial pressure and smear campaigns. Western Sahara is not peripheral to its findings.

The organisation devotes a case study to Sahrawi activists and reports that a former member of Morocco’s domestic intelligence service, identified as “Safir,” described Sahrawis and Riffians as priority intelligence targets, including beyond Morocco. Amnesty says it independently verified his identity, employment and key elements of his testimony.

The report also contains forensic evidence involving Pegasus spyware and documents cases connected to Sahrawi activism that reached European territory.

The people Amnesty examined are the tip of the iceberg. They are documented cases: people researchers could interview, devices they could examine, or targets for whom other evidence was available.

Surveillance is secret by design. Most people never learn that their phones have been compromised, and most suspicious devices will never reach a forensic laboratory.

That is why the chronology matters.

Chilling effect

On 8 April 2021, The Guardian quoted my warning that Sahrawi activists’ “phones and internet connections are hacked.” We were describing the symptoms years before Amnesty’s latest investigation exposed more of the machinery.

But surveillance is not simply about collecting information.

When a security service knows who an activist speaks to, where that person travels and what exists inside a phone, information can become power.

Amnesty documents cases in which private information gathered through surveillance later appeared in media coverage and coordinated smear campaigns against human rights defenders.

The organisation is careful: it could not independently establish the source of every piece of private material published. But it says the nature of some material raises serious concerns that surveillance-derived information may have reached media actors.

For Sahrawis, that raises an obvious question: How does private information about activists move from their lives and devices into the public sphere?

That question deserves independent forensic investigation.

But Amnesty’s report should provoke another examination — this one in Washington and European capitals.

For decades, Western governments have built close security relationships with Morocco around counterterrorism, intelligence cooperation, migration and regional stability.

The question is not whether those relationships should exist. It is whether the West has adequately examined what happens to security capabilities once they are in the hands of its partners.

Read more

Sánchez and the EU have decided that Morocco relations are too big to fail

Amnesty does not establish that every security capability Morocco obtained through Western cooperation was used against Sahrawis. The evidence does not support such a sweeping conclusion.

It does, however, justify harder questions.

What safeguards accompanied security cooperation? Who monitored end use? What happens when capabilities developed or acquired in an environment shaped by counterterrorism are directed toward peaceful human rights activism?

That is the line separating security from repression.

Western Sahara struggle

The contradiction is especially striking because Sahrawi human rights activism has often relied on peaceful means: demonstrations, documentation, journalism and engagement with international institutions.

Amnesty reports restrictions on expression and assembly concerning Sahrawi rights, alongside reports of arbitrary arrests, prolonged surveillance, restrictions affecting families and the dispersal of peaceful demonstrations.

Europe has encountered similar contradictions in its relationship with Morocco.

In June 2021, the European Parliament explicitly rejected Morocco’s use of border control and migration, particularly involving unaccompanied minors, as political pressure against Spain.

Yet the same resolution emphasised the longstanding relationship and cooperation between the European Union and Morocco in counterterrorism, migration and trade.

That contradiction should matter to Europeans.

When democratic governments make another state indispensable for stopping terrorism, controlling migration or providing intelligence, they provide more than resources. They provide leverage. Eventually, fear of losing cooperation can make scrutiny of a partner more difficult.

Europe has confronted another warning sign. In its response to the corruption scandal that engulfed the European Parliament, the Parliament itself denounced alleged attempts by Morocco and Qatar to influence lawmakers and staff through acts of corruption.

Read more

MEPs oppose including Morocco in Qatari corruption scandal

These remain allegations. They do not mean that every European position favourable to Morocco was corrupt. But they demonstrate why foreign influence over democratic institutions requires serious scrutiny.

European vs American foreign policy

Western Sahara remains an issue on the United Nations agenda and is tied to a decades-long international process concerning the political future of the territory.

That should matter to an EU that regularly invokes a rules-based international order.

Morocco has rejected previous allegations concerning Pegasus and described earlier Amnesty findings as baseless. Amnesty says it provided Moroccan authorities with a summary of its latest findings before publication and invited a response but received none before the report was published.

Those denials belong on the record.

So does the evidence.

The test of a human rights policy is not only how a democracy responds to abuses by its adversaries. The harder test is what it does when credible allegations concern a security partner.

For Sahrawis, however, this story is older than spyware.

For nearly half a century, generations of Sahrawis have lived through restrictions and documented abuses connected to political expression over the future of Western Sahara. Children have grown into adults watching what can happen when someone speaks publicly: surveillance, imprisonment, smear campaigns, pressure and fear.

After all these years, what Sahrawis are asking for is not complicated.

We are not asking the world to choose an answer for us. Nor should the outcome be written in advance in our favour.

We are asking for something more elementary: Treat the Sahrawi as a free human being, capable of thinking, choosing and expressing a view about the future of the land he or she calls home without fear.

It is easy to live in a democratic society, protected by freedom of expression and equality before the law, and then propose a political solution for a distant people who will have to live with its consequences every day.

But a human question should come before the geopolitical one:

Would you accept for yourself and your children a political order in which expressing your views about your homeland could expose you to surveillance, intimidation or punishment?

A Sahrawi is not a number in a diplomatic file, a detail in a geopolitical bargain or a security problem to be managed.

A Sahrawi is a human being, with a memory, a family, a homeland, an opinion and a future.

After nearly 50 years, perhaps it is time simply to hear that voice as it is, rather than as others interpret it.

Give Sahrawis one day without fear.

One day to speak without surveillance, without pressure and without wondering whether their words will reach their phone, their workplace, their home or their family.

Do not write the answer for them.

Just let them speak.

If any political solution is truly just, why should it fear the voice of the human being who will have to live under it?

]]> Cut the EU budget and we all lose https://euobserver.com/241660/cut-the-eu-budget-and-we-all-lose/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:19:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241660 As national leaders call for massive cuts in the next EU budget, the parliament’s budget chiefs, MEP Siegfried Mureşan and Carla Tavares, warn that slashing EU cash now will undercut Europe’s competitiveness, security and social safety net for years to come.]]> When certain governments discuss the EU’s next seven-year budget, their first reflex seems to be: what can we cut? That is the wrong question. The real question is not how much the EU budget costs, but how much an insufficient budget will cost us all.  

Economic benefits of EU membership are estimated to be two to six times the financial contribution of individual member states. For every euro we contribute to the EU budget, we can receive up to six euros in return.

That is the power of investing together: European investment delivers more than fragmented national spending. And it does so with a budget of just one percent of EU GNI, while national budgets can reach 50 percent.

The EU budget is not simply money transferred from national capitals to Brussels: it is an investment that creates value benefiting citizens through stronger economies, better infrastructure, food security, cutting-edge research, educational opportunities, regional development, and security.

Ultimately, all member states benefit from the added value created by the EU, making the concept of ‘net contributors’ obsolete.

Easing the pressure on national contributions is a legitimate objective, and it has a clear solution: an EU revenue reform. 

Read more

Von der Leyen joins MEPs in defence of EU’s €2 trillion spending plan ahead of summit

The European Parliament supports the basket approach of the European Commission on new own resources and its proposals. It also proposed three additional options capable of generating substantial revenue by 1 January 2028: a digital service levy on major platforms (€25.2bn per year), a levy on online gambling (€3.9bn per year) and a crypto-assets-based own resource (€3bn per year).

Our position is clear: large global companies that benefit most from Europe’s single market should contribute fairly to the EU budget that makes those benefits possible.

Cutting the EU budget may look like saving money. But if it means weaker competitiveness, less social investment and a less secure Europe, we save nothing and taxpayers foot the bill.

Read more

EU 40% development aid cut would be ‘drastic betrayal’ of values, says top MEP

The European Union’s common budget has not grown in real terms for 40 years. On the contrary, its purchasing power has been steadily eroded due to high inflation. The current EU budget has lost around 10 percent of its purchasing power compared to when it was adopted in 2020. 

A more ambitious EU budget does not automatically mean that member states will have to contribute substantially more from their national budgets. When amounts are compared in constant prices and as a share of the size of the European economy – like with like – a more realistic picture emerges. 

In terms of spending capacity, and without counting repayment of the Covid-19 recovery fund (NextGenerationEU), the commission’s proposal for the 2028-2034 budget would be below the relative size of the current 2021-2027 MFF at the time of its adoption.

Even with parliament’s proposed increase for key EU programmes, member states’ contributions would still not substantially increase. 

Read more

Frugal EU states seeking budget cuts are shooting their own regions in the foot

Let us not forget: Europeans benefit considerably more than their countries’ headline contributions suggest. The single market is the clearest example. By removing barriers between 27 economies, it creates opportunities and delivers growth that no country could generate alone. 

By reducing the budget, the EU and its member states will have less capacity to deliver the economic and social benefits that citizens expect. We’ll have less cohesion, less competitiveness, a weaker agricultural sector, less global influence, reduced social investment and a much less secure Europe. And this also comes at a cost. A big one.

Instead of “what can we cut” we should be asking ourselves, “how can we finance a budget that delivers more for all”.  

If we genuinely want to use limited public resources efficiently, we must invest together. Economies of scale work for successful businesses, and they work for Europe.

Siegfried Mureşan (EPP, Romania) and Carla Tavares (S&D, Portugal) are the parliament’s co-rapporteurs on the EU budget, also known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF)

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

France has been seeing growing protests by high school and university students in recent weeks.

The movement is continuing today with a fourth day of mobilisation. According to the government, the far-left opposition party is fuelling the protests. For Donald Trump, the movement is the result of mass migration and the presence of Islam.

But what are young people actually protesting about? High school students’ anger has been building for some time. One of the tipping points came in June, when temperatures inside many schools rose above 35 degrees. Many classrooms had no fans, let alone air conditioning.

And this happened in buildings that were already often in poor condition. Add to that the fact that absent teachers are frequently not replaced. The result was what you might call a general overheating — both literally and politically.

Read more

Listen: One year out, could the far-right win France’s 2027 election?

The government, meanwhile, has accused the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed, or LFI) of fuelling the protests. Some commentators have even suggested that the movement was orchestrated by the party from the beginning.

There is little doubt that LFI is supporting the mobilisation and may be trying to benefit politically from it. But dismissing the protests as political manipulation risks ignoring problems that are well documented.

As sociologist and child psychiatrist Laelia Benoit recently told Le Monde, assuming that high school students cannot think for themselves and must necessarily be manipulated by adults or political parties is, in her words, a way of denying them their ability to act politically.

And many of their demands are supported by both parents and teachers. Teachers, for example, have long complained about the lack of replacements when they are absent.

Read more

How bad does it have to get for the ECB to save France?

This is supported by the latest PISA report on France: 87% of French students — as well as school principals — said their school’s capacity to teach was affected by a lack of teachers.

So young people are increasingly asking to be heard. Earlier this week, they put forward their demands, resulting in 10 concrete measures supported by both high school and university students.

Among other things, they are calling for a major programme to renovate schools, more staff, a guaranteed €1 meal at university canteens, and higher housing benefits and grants so that students can live with dignity.

So what is the government offering in response? France has opened an online platform in recent days where students can submit their demands. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said yesterday that the platform had already received more than 40,000 contributions.

So for now, the government’s message is essentially: go back to class and submit your demands online. The prime minister then pointed to the additional €1 billion he has proposed for the education budget next year.

And as for more immediate measures, he announced five areas of work that should begin at the end of October. They include tackling teacher replacements, improving schools’ material conditions, reorganising school timetables, reforming the university admissions platform which appears to be a nightmare, and thinking about how to give high school students a greater voice.

Let’s see if that is enough to ease the protests.

]]> Germany’s most promising industries depend on China, clashing with Berlin’s derisking push, study finds https://euobserver.com/241603/germanys-most-promising-industries-depend-on-china-despite-berlins-derisking-push-study-finds/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 04:33:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241603 Small electrical firms best placed to drive Germany's industrial renewal rely on China as their main supplier, competitor and sometimes customer, leaving Berlin with a dilemma: the fastest way to scale them up is with the very Chinese components it wants to reduce reliance on. ]]> Germany’s most promising industries are also among the most tightly connected to Chinese supply chains, found a new study published on Thursday (8 October).

The paper, Industry with a Future, by the Cologne-based ZOE Institute for Future-fit Economies, ranks 62 German industries according to their prospects for future value, links to green technologies, and contribution to the wider German economy.

Small electrical industries come out particularly well, including clean tech sectors, such as battery producers and manufacturers of electric motors, switchboards, and computer equipment. 

These areas combine the kind of specialised know-how that is difficult to copy, which can protect high-wage economies, such as Germany, from cheap foreign competition into the future. 

But many of those industries still depend on China for components, and in some cases also rely on Chinese buyers to sell their products to. 

“China matters to these industries not only as a competitor, but also as a supplier and a buyer,” the ZOE Institute study’s co-author, Marla Schiefeling, told journalists at a briefing on Wednesday.

That leaves Germany with a difficult industrial policy problem: It needs to scale these sectors up while cutting its dependence on China, but the fastest way to scale is with cheap Chinese components.

To solve this predicament, the authors argue for diversifying suppliers and creating more demand in Germany and the EU.

Old giants, new tricks? 

The driver of the troubles is that the German economic model itself isn’t working anymore. 

Around 420,000 manufacturing jobs were lost between 2019 and 2025, and German exports to China fell 29 percent from their 2021 peak to 2025, the study notes. 

“Production and employment in German industry have been falling for years. This is definitely not a cyclical dip. It is a structural problem,” said co-author Lukas Bertram. 

Reliant as it is on exports, Germany’s big export industries, such as car makers or industrial machines, are losing competitiveness, mostly to China, while facing US tariffs abroad and high energy prices at home.

Yet the study argues these industries are also the country’s best hope, and are better placed to create new value than their current troubles suggest.

German carmakers, such as BMW, Mercedes, and Volkswagen, which are in the direct line of fire of China’s EV dominance, already have many of the industrial capabilities to make much of what is needed to build batteries, wind turbines or power grids, from electronics to specialised metal parts. 

“From these capabilities, new leading roles can emerge, for instance in electric mobility,” the report’s authors note.

While still associated with fuel and combustion engines, carmaking ranks among the top three industries for eight of the 10 green supply chains the authors examined.

Machinery, metal products and parts of the chemicals industry also do well, which the authors initially found surprising. 

“We briefly wondered whether something was off with the methodology. But once we dug deeper, we realised it makes complete sense,” said Schiefeling.

“There’s still a lot of potential and a huge amount of technological know-how there,” she added.

“The task is to translate that into sustainable production structures from which new value can emerge,” she said.

Other sectors, such as coal power, coke ovens, oil refining, and fertiliser production, by contrast, have little future in Germany, the study finds.

But rather than letting them collapse, the authors argue they should be wound down gradually, which they call “strategic de-scaling.” 

‘Made in EU’

Meanwhile in Brussels, the debate about the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act is heating up.

The first version of the plan was circulated by the commission in March, but it is still being redrafted, with a new version presented on Wednesday. 

At the heart of the plan is the ‘Made in EU’ clause. This would require governments to favour European-made (low-carbon) goods, starting with steel, cement, aluminium, cars, and clean technologies. 

In a joint non-paper sent to the commission on Monday, German chancellor Friedrich Merz and French president Emmanuel Macron similarly called for a “European preference” in strategic sectors and to “derisk” from Chinese supply chains, notably in batteries and clean energy equipment. 

But the ZOE Institute’s Bertram said that while ‘made in Europe’ criteria could help create demand for EU and Germany fledgeling industries, this might not help all sectors concerned.

For a German battery or switchboard maker that can only source its parts from China, such rules might “initially raise prices rather than genuinely create local production capacity,” he said. 

This piece was amended for clarity.

]]> Broken promise of ‘European solution’ on migration overshadows next week’s summit https://euobserver.com/241582/broken-promise-of-european-solution-on-migration-overshadows-next-weeks-summit/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241582 EU leaders have run out of ideas as they keep rehashing the same solutions on migration.]]> Twelve years ago, EU summit leaders announced they had a strategy to tackle unprecedented migrant arrivals.

Next week, they will meet again in Brussels and to tell us something similar.

We journalists will report on the latest twists and turns, hoping to get some sort of angle that hasn’t been covered. But the reality is that our leaders have broadly failed.

Dozens of EU summit conclusions have been published since 2015, when one around million Syrians arrived in Europe to seek protection.

We need stronger external borders to preserve the Schengen passport-free zone, they said. We need partnerships with foreign states to save lives. We need to step up deportations. We need a European solution.

All of these ideas and strategies have found a home in council conclusions, in various iterations, since 2015. All of them.

Some have actually panned out, including an EU migrant swap deal with Turkey and other deals with autocrats in Tunisia, Egypt and elsewhere. Others like internal reforms on asylum have also been delivered.

Yet the sense of urgency to tackle these issues continues because there is an obvious disconnect between what has been delivered, the promises made and the lived experience on the ground.

People still come. Some 80,000 arrived in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta end of July alone.

Many are still fleeing violence, war and economic hardships. Others are lured by the promise of labour in Europe by Europeans willing to exploit them.

I remember meeting a group of boys from Bangladesh on the Ocean Viking, freshly rescued in the middle of the night, asking when they would be able to start working in Italy.

One of them was still shaking with fear and sobbing, following a near death experience.

Read more

Ocean Viking’s largest ever rescue – witnessed first-hand

The European Commission is now claiming that the drop of irregular arrivals is due to their migration policy reforms, as if the fall of the murderous Assad regime in Syria had no discernible impact.

Perhaps some of that is true. But there is no disputing that Syrians accounted for over 100,000 irregular crossings in 2023, a year before Assad fell. It then dropped to around 6,000. Today, it is around 1,000, according to Frontex.

At some point, one has to wonder if these conclusions, repeated ad nauseam, is nothing but political theatre by a leadership that has run out of ideas.

    ]]>         Sanctions in February, handshakes in September: EU’s flip-flop Iran policy is putting lives at risk https://euobserver.com/241462/sanctions-in-february-handshakes-in-september-eus-flip-flop-iran-policy-is-putting-lives-at-risk/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 10:42:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241462 By sitting down with senior Iranian figures who publicly back the Revolutionary Guard while keeping sanctions limited to technocratic lists, EU governments risk undermining their own leverage at a time of rising regional tensions.]]> Why would the European Union list the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organisation in February, and then, seven months later, have its top diplomat sit down with the foreign minister of the government the Guard Corps defends?

    At the UN General Assembly last month, EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas met Abbas Araghchi, who served in the Guard Corps during the Iran–Iraq war.

    Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten met president Masoud Pezeshkian, who in 2019 joined fellow parliamentarians in wearing the Guard Corps uniform to protest Washington’s terrorist designation of it. France, Italy, and Norway held meetings of their own.

    These talks came less than nine months after Iranian security forces, on 8 and 9 January, killed protesters on a scale without precedent in the country’s modern history.

    The human rights group HRANA has verified more than 7,000 deaths, and the UN special rapporteur warned that the toll may exceed 20,000.

    In September, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that the crackdown amounted to crimes against humanity. Nor has the killing stopped: Iran Human Rights counted at least 532 executions in the first eight months of this year, including protesters arrested in January.

    After a massacre, a foreign policy guided by European values should pursue one aim above others: making a repetition more costly for those who would order and carry it out.

    Naming and shaming raises the reputational cost of repression, targeted sanctions raise its material cost, and delegitimisation raises the political cost of staying loyal to the regime.

    They work only in combination, since sanctions without delegitimization tell the regime’s elite that their assets are at risk, but their standing is not.

    Read more

    Why the Iran uprising is Europe’s strategic blind spot

    EU vs US sanctions

    Europe has used the first two instruments. The EU listed the Guard Corps in February and sanctioned additional Iranian officials for human rights abuses.

    However, these measures target assets and individuals, while the government that presided over the killing keeps its seat at the top table.

    The UNGA in New York showed how little the third instrument has been used.

    The terrorist listing freezes the Guard Corps’ funds. Neither Araghchi nor Pezeshkian is on an EU sanctions list.

    Yet it leaves a question unanswered: how far should the logic of a terrorist designation extend to the government that funds and publicly defends it?

    Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union requires the Union’s external action to be guided by human rights and to be consistent.

    Branding the Guard Corps a terrorist organisation in Brussels while posing for photographs with the government it defends in New York sits uneasily with that obligation.

    This inconsistency is costly. In a study in foreign policy analysis, my co-authors and I examined how Iranians reacted to US sanctions. Comprehensive sanctions produced a rally around the government, even among reformists.

    The 2019 designation of the Guard Corps, by contrast, produced almost no rally outside the regime’s hardliner core. Thus, targeted pressure on the security apparatus does not drive Iranians into its arms.

    Handshakes, on the other hand, may give the apparatus exactly what targeted sanctions are meant to withhold: international legitimacy.

    The photographs from New York reach two audiences.

    The first sits inside the state: an officer deciding whether to fire on a crowd, or to step aside, weighs one question above most others, namely whether the regime will survive, and each of those photographs suggests an answer.

    The second audience is the families of those killed, executed, and blinded since January. For them, the message is that Europe has moved on after eight months.

    Read more

    Reporting when the internet goes dark

    A picture is worth a thousand words

    I am not against diplomacy. Kallas raised the sharp rise in executions with Araghchi, and Jetten raised human rights and Iranian actions on Dutch soil with Pezeshkian. Channels on shipping, detained Europeans, and de-escalation should stay open.

    My objection concerns the level and the format: a meeting between leaders, photographed at the General Assembly with no public conditions attached, is not a technical channel.

    Concerns voiced in private do not travel as far as the photograph, which signals normal relations with a government that has done nothing to earn them.

    Four steps would help.

    First, the Council should agree on a common line: contact at the technical and envoy level, and leader-level meetings only on public conditions, beginning with a halt to protest-related executions.

    Second, human rights sanctions should move up the chain of command, to those who answer politically for the security forces.

    Third, member states should invest in accountability that does not depend on Tehran, such as universal jurisdiction cases and evidence-sharing with the UN mission.

    Finally, Europe should engage openly with Iran’s democratic opposition.

    The EU has already decided, in law, what the Guard Corps is. Its leaders have yet to act accordingly. A massacre answered with sanctions in February and handshakes in September does not raise the cost of the next one. It lowers it.

When big corporations emerged, corporate and payroll taxes followed. When mass car ownership took hold, fuel duties emerged to pay for the roads it required. 

    As AI shifts work from people to machines, it will force a rethink of who gets taxed, on what, and where. Nowhere is that question more urgent than in Europe, which funds the world’s most comprehensive welfare states primarily through taxes on work.

    Taxes on work make up 51.5 percent of all tax revenue in the EU-27, according to the European Commission’s latest Taxation Trends data — a share that rose in 2024. These charges are taken straight from the payslip. They’re hard to avoid, and scale with employment.

    AI, by replacing human work with software and machines, eats away at exactly this tax base. 

    The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates that around 40 percent of jobs worldwide are exposed to AI. If that leads to fewer workers, it will also mean fewer payslips, pension contributions and social charges, weakening the revenue streams that fund Europe’s pension and healthcare systems. This is not a distant problem; the costs are already mounting.

    Read more

    EU not ‘lagging’ US in AI-productivity gains, Lagarde tells MEPs

    Shift the burden to corporate profits

    The obvious response is to shift more of the tax burden onto corporate profits, which will increasingly reflect the gains firms make by deploying AI instead of hiring workers.

    Unlike a tax on machines and equipment themselves, a profit tax falls mostly on excess profits and need not distort investment. The case for shifting weight from payroll taxes to profits is strong and strengthens as AI replaces more workers with machines.

    But profits, unlike payrolls, move. A company can locate its intellectual property in a low-rate jurisdiction — a pattern Europe knows well from decades of profits routed through Ireland and Luxembourg — and ensure that profits are booked far from where the jobs are lost. It is how the world’s largest technology and AI firms already operate.

    Read more

    Reverse centaurs: EU approach to AI risks dystopia for human workers

    Two-pillar answer

    The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD’s) Inclusive Framework was designed to address exactly this: profits shifted across jurisdictions to avoid tax, and e-commerce allowed sales where firms have no physical presence. AI makes these reforms more urgent. 

    Pillar One of the framework put forward by the Paris-based wealthy nations’ club addresses where a corporation is taxed. It shifts partial taxing rights for the largest multinationals away from where they are headquartered and toward where their customers and users are located. 

    Still under negotiation, it would apply only to a handful of the largest firms, but many AI companies would qualify. 

    These firms are concentrated in a select number of countries, very few of them European, but the displacement they cause, and the public services that displaced workers will require, will weigh heavily on European budgets.

    Pillar Two of the OECD framework introduces a global minimum corporate tax of 15 percent on multinationals with revenues above €750m.

    The EU moved first and furthest: Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523 made the minimum tax binding across the Union from 2024, and 22 of the 27 member states now apply it in full. The United States, notably, has not implemented the rules. 

    Read more

    Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

    Politics is undermining the fix

    But the obstacles are real. US ratification of the OECD proposals is unlikely, and many of the largest companies are headquartered there. 

    The pressure is already reshaping Europe’s own rules: under the G7’s June 2025 ‘side-by-side’ agreement, US-parented groups would be exempt from the EU’s minimum-tax rules: a carveout the European Commission confirmed in January 2026 and which several member states consider legally fragile. 

    The Commission also dropped its proposed EU digital levy under US trade pressure, leaving a patchwork of national digital services taxes in France, Italy, Spain, Austria, and elsewhere.

    Such exceptions and carveouts show that big-power politics can hollow out the framework. These reforms were designed to address the tax challenges for an AI-economy. They were good policy then. They are fiscal necessities now. Fairer corporate taxation will not be enough, but it is a start. 

    Europe’s choice

    The EU has instruments on the table, the BEFIT common corporate tax base and the proposed Corporate Resource for Europe, but both remain politically contested.

    European governments that fail to act will be managing the social costs of technological disruption with a tax system built for the industrial age, while the profits that fund their rivals accumulate beyond their reach.

    Even if Europeans work less, their needs for health care, pensions, and consumption remain. As wage-based contributions shrink, Europe must shift more of the tax burden onto corporate profits and close off the routes that let those profits move beyond the reach of the states bearing the costs of automation. 

    Productivity gains may soften the arithmetic; they will not repeal it. The tax base must follow the economy.

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Chinese carmakers are taking an increasing share of the European car market, particularly when it comes to electric vehicles. Why are European carmakers now opening their factories to their Chinese competitors?

    Until recently, the main concern in Europe was Chinese-made electric vehicles being imported into the EU. That’s why, two years ago, the EU imposed hefty tariffs on Chinese electric cars.

    But Chinese manufacturers have found another way into the European market: they are setting up production here. Some are building factories of their own. Others are entering partnerships with European carmakers and using their existing production sites.

    Read more

    THIS WEEK: EU trade chief heads to China as Brussels unveils long-delayed pre-enlargement reforms

    That’s the case with Stellantis and Chinese manufacturer Leapmotor. And now Dongfeng is also negotiating to produce cars at the French plant of Rennes La Janais. Because by moving production to Europe, Chinese manufacturers may be losing one of their main advantages, which is cheap labour.

    But low labour costs are only one part of their competitive edge.

    Chinese manufacturers also continue to benefit from state support. And setting up production in Europe doesn’t necessarily mean building brand-new factories.

    In many cases, Chinese companies are looking to partner with European manufacturers and use factories that are already there — factories that are no longer operating at full capacity. That means they can save significantly on investment costs. And they can also rely on their European partners’ existing sales and distribution networks.

    So how big is this Chinese presence in Europe becoming? For 2028, there are already 12 projects involving Chinese carmakers setting up production in Europe. Several are in Spain, with others in France, Belgium, Slovakia, Hungary, Sweden and Austria.

    Read more

    [Interview] EU’s carmakers face their own Nokia challenge to survive Chinese threat, says industry expert

    Now, why would European manufacturers allow their Chinese competitors to produce cars in their own factories? Part of the answer is that European carmakers are struggling to keep up in electric vehicles sells. And that is contributing to factory closures and job losses.

    European manufacturers have to meet EU targets on average CO2 emissions each year. And producing more electric vehicles is necessary to meet those requirements.

    So partnerships with Chinese manufacturers can serve two purposes: they can help European companies fulfilling their green cars objectives, while also keeping existing factories and jobs running.

    Though there is a longer-term risk for European manufacturers. The more Chinese companies establish themselves in Europe, the more competitive pressure they could put on European brands — potentially even leading to takeovers. That has happened before: Volvo Cars, for example, was acquired by Chinese group Geely in 2010. 

    In Germany, carmakers are for now refusing to open the doors of their production sites to the Chinese. But they do have partnerships with Chinese companies to produce vehicles in China, where they can benefit from lower production costs. That explains why they were very much opposed to imposing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.

    Read more

    Volkswagen benefited from €1.5bn in German EV subsidies as it lobbies EU to hit Chinese cars harder

    But the situation is now changing. Volkswagen closed its Dresden factory last year, and other German plants are also facing closure risks. Germany’s car industry is therefore increasingly joining calls for stronger protection against Chinese competition.

    And that brings us back to the Franco-German paper that is circulating in Brussels, which calls for measures to restrict Chinese access to the European market.

    Because this debate goes well beyond cars. The EU is increasingly concerned about Chinese competition and dependence in a range of strategic industries. This will be discussed next week, when EU leaders meet in Brussels.

    The European Commission could also present a new so-called “diversification” tool, either at the summit or around it. One possibility would be to require companies not to rely exclusively on China for certain critical materials. Something which could trigger what we call a trade war. I’ll be following that very closely!

Simplification must go hand-in-hand with legal certainty https://euobserver.com/241094/eu-inc-simplification-must-go-hand-in-hand-with-legal-certainty/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241094 Europe is about to create a form of company that no public authority will be able to check in substance. Speed is not the same as trust. With the European Parliament and the Council finalising their positions, the Notaries of Europe urge legislators to strengthen its safeguards.]]>

    This article is paid for by Council of the Notariats of the European Union (CNUE).

    An address rented in a European capital, an electronic signature obtained online, a 48-hour waiting period.

    Under the proposed regulation establishing a 28th company law regime, known as ‘EU Inc.’, this could be enough to establish a company with legal personality throughout the European Union.

    No share capital would be required. The founder could complete the entire process without appearing, even digitally, before a public authority or another person entrusted with preventive legal control.

    There would be no personal verification of their legal capacity, of whether they understand what they are signing, or of whether they are acting on behalf of someone who wishes to remain invisible.

    The company could then open bank accounts, enter into contracts, own assets and employ people across the European Union. If the company later fails to meet its obligations, creditors and employees may find that there are no assets to recover and that the person formally responsible for it was acting merely as a front man. 

    Read more

    Unions rally against new ‘EU Inc’ race-to-bottom on labour laws and pay

    This scenario illustrates the serious concerns raised by the proposal for a Regulation on ‘EU Inc.’ put forward by the European Commission and currently being examined by the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union.

    The preventive checks set out in Article 14 of the commission’s proposal are largely limited to formal requirements.

    There is no independent and impartial scrutiny of the founders’ legal capacity, of the lawfulness of the articles of association, or of whether the transaction complies with substantive legal requirements. Transfers of shares and capital transactions are also not subject to substantive control. Liquidation is treated primarily as an administrative formality, even though it can directly affect creditors and employees.

    The consequences may extend far beyond company law.

    Companies own real estate and are entered in land registers. If it is no longer possible to establish reliably who owns a company, it also becomes more difficult to establish who ultimately owns the real estate held by that company. Reliable company information therefore matters for the transparency of property ownership.

    ‘Not reliably verified’?

    If the information in a register has not been reliably verified, others have to verify it themselves. Banks, business partners and investors may need additional legal opinions, audits and insurance. Costs that a preventive check avoids at the outset may therefore arise repeatedly at a later stage.

    Read more

    EU unveils ’28th regime’, creating bloc-wide business code

    This would represent a shift from the European tradition of public preventive legal control towards a model that relies more heavily on resolving disputes after they arise.

    Delaware is a prominent example of such an approach, supported by specialised courts and a correspondingly prominent role for litigation. Transplanting it to Europe would place additional demands on national judicial systems that lack the necessary resources.

    Read more

    MEPs back new EU‑wide ‘28th regime’ businesses plan — but fear a ‘European Delaware’

    The proposal also raises questions with regard to the recent European efforts to combat money laundering and the financing of terrorism.

    The creation of the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) is the latest milestone in this process. To create, at the very same time, a legal form with significantly reduced checks risks severely undermining these efforts.

    The same applies to sanctions: their enforcement depends on knowing who is really behind a company – especially when shares are transferred. Without reliable legality control of share transfers, corporate ownership can change unnoticed and become a vehicle for sanctions circumvention.

    The amendments required are straightforward. The acquis of European company law, as established by Directive (EU) 2017/1132 and recently reinforced by Directive (EU) 2025/25, should also apply to EU Inc. companies.

    This means reliable identification of founders and directors, public oversight of legal compliance at the time of formation and at subsequent stages, and reliable business registers. 

    Public protection

    These safeguards exist for a reason.

    They protect not only the parties to a transaction, but the public at large. Because they serve a public purpose, they must remain a public responsibility. Private service providers cannot replace independent preventive control carried out under public responsibility. 

    How these checks are organised differs between member states. In some member states, public authorities carry them out directly. In others, the state entrusts notaries with this public function.

    Notarial involvement therefore does not add another layer of control: the same public function is simply carried out by different public authorities. In many member states, a company can already be formed digitally within 48 hours, with full legal verification carried out by a public official.

    The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union will decide their positions in the coming weeks.

    There is still time to improve the legislative framework of EU Inc. significantly and to make it a success.

    This requires digital and efficient procedures without compromising legal certainty. The rule of law is one of the European Union’s strengths. EU Inc. should build on that strength, not weaken it.

    The head of the French central bank, Emmanuel Moulin, told the Financial Times that his country risks being “strangled by interest rates”.

    The best solution, he made clear, was for the French government to cut costs and reduce the deficit, which, in an unchanged scenario, could reach upwards of six percent next year.

    Last week, the French minority government proposed €43bn worth of cuts for 2027. But pushing them through parliament is a tall order in a divided country.

    Meanwhile, investors are dumping French bonds, pushing up French government borrowing costs compared to German benchmark Bunds. This is already immensely costly to French society.

    “In three weeks, we’ve lost the equivalent of €15bn a year in higher debt-servicing costs over a 10-year horizon, or almost €100bn cumulatively over 10 years!”, French economist Shahin Vallée said on social media last week.

    The gap, or spread, between French and German bond yields, historically around 50 basis points (0.5 percentage points), was 109 basis points when he wrote it on Wednesday. It is now 30 points higher.

    Spreads are a crucial marker for financial stability because they show how nervous investors are. The bigger the spread, the higher the perceived risk.

    And France’s parabolic bond spread is already bringing back unwelcome memories of the eurozone crisis in November 2011, when the spread reached 200 basis points.

    Bypass parliament?

    The question is what to do about it, and who is best positioned to act. The French government could bypass a parliamentary vote or push through the budget by ordinance, under articles 49.3 and 47 of the constitution, respectively.

    “I would like to caution against large cuts. It would risk cutting deep into critical priorities that we all together have agreed on,” von der Leyen told MEPs during a speech in Strasbourg on Tuesday (6 October), ahead of an EU summit on 15 October.

    The commission has proposed a budget worth just under €2 trillion, equivalent to 1.26 percent of the EU’s gross national income, a small increase on the previous seven year spending plan. But the so-called ‘frugal’ group of countries, led by Germany, have demanded hefty cuts, complaining that they are contributing too much. 

    “Having no new financial framework is by far the most financially advantageous solution for Germany,” chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Monday. 

    But 17 EU countries from Southern and Eastern Europe signed a joint letter last week, demanding that farmers’ subsidies via the Common Agricultural Policy are maintained, as well as spending across the EU’s poorest regions, known as cohesion policy 

    During a press conference on Tuesday, Siegfried Muresan, the Romanian centre-right MEP who is co-leading parliament’s negotiating team on the seven-year budget with Portuguese socialist and democrat Claudia Tavares, said that there was “still time” for the Irish presidency to avoid proposing “unjustified cuts” that “would make Europe weaker and severely undermine the institutional cooperation between parliament and council.” 

    Though Muresan conceded that governments did not want to increase their national contributions, “there is a way out”, he said.

      <title>Skepticism mires Trump’s Iowa steel plant project: ‘Promises are not the same as jobs’</title>

      <description><p>The project has sparked doubts over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s record</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> has long sought to portray himself as a man of steel, from the White House <a href="https://x.com/WhiteHouse/status/1943493150644777199">photoshopping </a>Trump to look like Superman, to enacting tariffs on steel and approving the sale of US Steel to Japan’s Nippon Steel with a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jun/18/nippon-steel-acquires-us-steel">”golden” share</a> given to the US government.</p><p>Most recently, the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/trump-administration">Trump administration</a> announced plans to construct the largest steel plant in the US, a $15bn plant in Lee county, Iowa, to be built by India-based Mesabi Metallics.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/07/trump-steel-plant-iowa-skepticism">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Suit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information</p><p>McDonald’s is facing a lawsuit in federal court over its alleged use of an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">AI</a> tool to determine pricing across independent franchises, which prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for Americans.</p><p>The vast majority of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/mcdonalds">McDonald’s</a> US stores are independently owned and are said to individually decide on prices under company policy.       <description><p>The findings come after warnings from tech leaders that AI placed in the wrong hands could trigger larger threats such as nuclear war or bioweaponry destruction</p><p>Misusing <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">artificial intelligence</a> (AI) is the top threat to companies’ reputations – more so than being accused of putting children in the way of mental, emotional or physical harm and issues exposed by the US-Israel war on Iran, among other brand risks, according to a new survey of more than 150 public affairs leaders.</p><p>Those findings in the new edition of the quarterly Reputation Risk Index, released on Tuesday, came on the heels of other perhaps more dire warnings from leading tech figures that AI in the wrong hands could <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/commentisfree/2026/sep/23/how-would-ai-actually-kill-all-humans-here-are-the-top-five-most-likely-scenarios">precipitate</a> existential threats on a mass scale such as nuclear war or destruction by bioweaponry.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/06/ai-misuse-brand-reputation">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world</p><p>Donald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities, <a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117269745153543631">writing on Truth Social</a>: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”</p><p>But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one that <a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117213056648777213">raised the possibility of cutting off all trade</a> with dozens of the US’s trading partners.       <title>Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax</link>
      <description><p>An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight? </p><p>Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “<a href="https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/millionaires-tax-faq/">millionaire tax</a>” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-signs-millionaires-tax-law">signed</a> into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.</p><p>An <a href="https://leg.wa.gov/media/ucubvqsd/2026-summary-of-initiative-26-645.pdf">initiative</a> on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A <a href="https://no645.com/our-coalition/">coalition</a> of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 08 Oct 2026 10:02:14 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Minister signalled Government was set to ‘renege’ on RTÉ deal in budget talks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/minister-signalled-government-was-set-to-renege-on-rte-deal-in-budget-talks/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/minister-signalled-government-was-set-to-renege-on-rte-deal-in-budget-talks/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Minister for Media Patrick O’Donovan warned before the budget that the Government would “renege” on its funding deal with RTÉ if more cash wasn’t found for his department.

In a letter last week, O’Donovan told Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers that, based on what was being offered, “the Government (not the Department) will renege on the three-year funding deal agreed with RTÉ in July 2024”.

In the final reckoning, an additional €21 million was allocated to O’Donovan’s department after the letter.

However, RTÉ’s allocation remained the same as 2026 at €240 million, €20 million less than it was expecting under a multi-year bailout deal between the then-government and the broadcaster.

The RTÉ funding allocation has sparked a major row between Montrose and the Government.

O’Donovan warned in his letter last Friday that based on the offer then on the table for his department, which stood at €827 million, RTÉ’s funding would in fact be cut by €11 million.

He also warned of funding consequences for a raft of other agencies including Sport Ireland and the Arts Council if no more money was forthcoming.

The final allocation to his department, which is responsible for culture and sport as well as media, was €848 million.

RTÉ says €20m cut in funding will impact on strategy as Minister criticises pace of reforms

It is understood that the budget ministers Chambers and Tánaiste Simon Harris, and Taoiseach Micheál Martin, believed that extra funding made available to the Department of Communications during tense budget negotiations over the weekend would solve any difficulties with the RTÉ allocation, but were only made aware of this issue on the day the budget was announced.

A Government source said “this only came to our attention yesterday [on budget day].”

On Wednesday O’Donovan denied that the move was a “cut” to RTÉ’s funding, despite the previous government promising to increase the broadcaster’s funding to €260 million next year.

“Over the lifetime of the three-year package of the bailout, it amounts to almost three-quarters of a billion euros,” he said. “That is an enormous amount of money from the taxpayers.”

He said he was not happy with the pace of change at the broadcaster and its transition to being a “more agile, smaller” organisation.

Minister calls for ‘cool heads’ in RTÉ funding dispute

In an email to staff, RTÉ director-general Kevin Bakhurst said he “completely rejects” O’Donovan’s assertion that the pace of reform at Montrose has been too slow.

Bakhurst said the station now had “some important decisions to make” if the previous agreement made with the government “will no longer be honoured”.

RTÉ reached a multi-year funding deal with the previous government in 2024. Under the agreement, the broadcaster would receive €725 million over three years: €225 million in 2025, €240 million in 2026, and €260 million in 2027.

Bakhurst told staff the decision to cut the funding for 2027 “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact our ability to deliver our five-year strategy.”

The station’s chairman, Terence O’Rourke, is seeking an urgent meeting with O’Donovan, RTÉ said.

It is understood O’Donovan is due to bring a memo to Cabinet in the coming weeks on future funding options for RTÉ.

Elsewhere, public sector unions said Budget 2027 was a missed opportunity for Chambers to signal his seriousness about preventing next week’s one day national strike.

Kevin Callinan, who chairs the Irish Congress of Trade Unions - and will lead the union side in negotiations to replace the expired public pay deal - said in the summer the unions would take account of whatever measures were in the budget when it came to framing their pay claim in talks. Callinan said on Wednesday the Minister had failed to “move the dial”.

TG4 and Screen Ireland budget funding amounts to ‘cut’ in real terms, industry warns

In the Dáil, the Taoiseach said a dispute “would be unwarranted given our willingness to talk”.

Some €1.2 billion has been set aside in the budget for a public pay deal. Martin said “there is no basis for industrial action or for disrupting people in education, health or anything else when this platform is there as a basis for negotiation on a new pay agreement”.

]]><![CDATA[Grafton to seek new board chair]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/grafton-to-seek-new-board-chair/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/grafton-to-seek-new-board-chair/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 07:35:44 +0000Builders merchant and DIY retailer Grafton is on the hunt for a new chair for its board.

The group said current chair Ian Tyler has informed the board he will step down, citing other commitments.

Tyler, who was previously chief executive of Balfour Beatty, joined Grafton’s board as a non-executive director in March 2024, and became chair following the 2024 annual general meeting.

He is also chair of BP and design and technical consulting firm BMT Group, and is senior independent director of Anglo American.

The London-listed group, which owns Woodies and Chadwicks, will now start the process to recruit a new chair.

It will be led by senior independent director Dr Rosheen McGuckian, with the assistance of an external search firm.

The company did not specify a timescale for the completion of the process.

]]><![CDATA[Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/06/consumers-can-save-up-to-50000-tax-free-in-new-personal-investment-accounts/Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:44:46 +0000People will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the Government new personal investment accounts, Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced in his Budget 2027 speech.

The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent. However, this tax will be levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000, not just the profit the account made over that year.

This holds out the prospect of people paying tax on their savings in years when they lost money simply because the balance of their account was above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.

Harris said the new accounts will be available from July 1st next year. About €170 billion is currently on deposit in Irish bank accounts, with the Minister having previously described that money as “sitting idle”.

Alongside the new accounts, the Minister announced a financial literacy campaign. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has set up a webpage that will allow people to read up about issues around investing, and the choices available.

It also offers a quick multiple choice self-assessment quiz that allows consumers to assess their investment readiness.

Irish households hold just 2.3 per cent of their financial assets in direct investments such as listed shares and debt securities, compared with an EU average of approximately 7.5 per cent.

Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day

The new scheme has been designed to encourage people to move their savings into market investments.

“The long-mooted investment account is an important step towards making long-term investment more accessible,” said Cróna Clohisey, director of members and advocacy at Chartered Accountants Ireland. “Now that the broad design has been announced, Government should move quickly to finalise the legislation, systems and guidance so that financial service providers can establish these accounts and people can begin using them.

“It is critical that there is no delay to the introduction timeline of mid-2027,” she said.

Michael Healy, chief executive of IG Consumer, said the Government had missed the chance to get Irish people investing.

“While the decision to set the tax-free threshold at €50,000 is better than we expected, it is a small victory within a fundamentally flawed model. The €12,000 annual contribution limit is far too low if the ambition is to get people investing seriously and building meaningful long-term wealth.

“But the bigger problem is the proposed 1 per cent annual tax on investments above the threshold,” said Healy. “Taxing the value of an investment rather than the return it generates means someone could face a tax bill even when their investments have fallen in value – effectively paying tax on losses. That is the wrong principle for an account designed to encourage people to invest.”

Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income

Robert Dever, head of tax at Eversheds Sutherland, agreed. The Government he said had adopted a cautious approach to the new scheme. “For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief arising on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account.”

However, Rory O’Brien, head of wealth management, Dublin, at Baker Tilly Ireland Wealth was more upbeat.

“On the whole, the new Irish Investment Account looks like a fantastic opportunity for those looking for better returns from the investment markets over the medium to long term to do so without being harshly punished when their investments do well. The opportunity for younger investors to start small and build up to the 50k without CGT is very positive and l would expect those looking to build deposits, to consider this as a viable option.”

The Government also announced a lowering of the rate of tax under the “deemed disposal” or exit tax regime that applies to investors in products currently available in the market.

Budget 2027 main points: Minimum wage to rise 79 cent; €12,000 per year limit for investment scheme

Last year, as part of Budget 2026, the deemed disposal tax rate was reduced from 41 per cent to 38 per cent. In 2024, a report by the Department of Finance into the funds sector advised the deemed disposal rule should be ended for exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and investment funds.

Exit tax is levied on profits when an investment is cashed in. Deemed disposal sees that tax levied every eight years after an investment is taken out, even if the investment is not cashed in.

Chartered Accountants Ireland’s Cróna Clohisey said it was “extremely disheartening that the eight-year deemed disposal rule remains. It has no place in a modern Irish investment landscape.

“Requiring people to pay tax on gains they have not realised undermines the benefits of long-term investment, adds unnecessary complexity for individual investors, and contradicts the wider Government drive to foster retail investment and encourage greater financial literacy.”

Irish Funds chairwoman, Andrea Kelly welcome dthe three point cut in the rate of tax but said the lack of any clear path to phasing out deemed disposal was “deeply disappointing”.

“The Government should now use the Finance Bill to provide the certainty that was missing from the Budget,” she said.

New accounts

Anyone over the age of 18 who is resident in the State and holds a PPS number can invest in the new personal investment scheme, but they can only have one account.

Eligible investments will include listed shares, listed bonds, financial instruments traded on a regulated market and a range of investment funds suitable for retail investors, including ETFs.

Investors will not be permitted to invest in what are deemed highly complex and risky products, including derivatives and crypto assets.

Catch up with all your Budget 2027 news here

There will be no minimum holding or lock-in period, and moving investment accounts between providers will be allowed, where possible, on a tax-neutral basis.

Any tax due will be calculated and paid at source by the companies providing the investment funds available under the scheme.

What is not yet clear is how much providers will charge for the products they offer.

Harris first announced his intention to introduce a new form of consumer-friendly investment account back in February.

He has returned to the theme regularly since then but, until Tuesday, had declined to confirm the amount that could be put into such accounts each month or year, the threshold above which the funds will be taxed, or the rate of taxation.

Harris’s department had examined similar types of accounts operating in other countries. Ultimately, it opted largely for the Swedish model despite strong industry lobbying in favour of the rival UK individual savings account (ISA) model.

]]>Neil Hall<![CDATA[Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/07/qa-budget-childcare-package-has-parents-in-a-spin-whats-in-it/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/07/qa-budget-childcare-package-has-parents-in-a-spin-whats-in-it/Wed, 07 Oct 2026 15:05:33 +0000Childcare is among the big bills for any young family, so it was not surprising that the budget announcement that the cost of care would fall next year to €550 a month per child from €735 attracted a lot of attention. What was announced in the budget?

Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said he was reducing the “maximum childcare fees paid by parents from €735 to €550 per month” for children up to senior infants from September of next year.

How is he doing that?

The Government is increasing the universal subsidy payable under the National Childcare Scheme to €2.50 an hour from €2.14. That subsidy is payable for care of up to 45 hours per week.

He also said he was reducing the maximum weekly fee cap that childcare facilities operating under the State’s core funding system can charge to €250 from €280.

What would that mean for parents?

The Minister said the measure would save parents €2,220 annually per child, a significant saving from after-tax income.

How much?

How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents

What’s happening there?

Not for the first time, there appears to be a substantial “reality gap” between the Government’s understanding of the “maximum” cost of care and the real maximum under its own core funding rules.

The amount childcare providers can charge is divided into bands based on the hours of care provided. The Minister’s figures are based on Band E, covering children in care for between 40 and 50 hours a week.

The issue is that most parents – certainly in and around Dublin – are paying under Band F, for children in care for 50 or more hours, which is significantly more expensive.

As 50 hours a week is almost 10 hours a day, how come children are in care that long or longer?

The issue is not so much how long they are in care as how many hours the providers have to stay open. In urban areas and the commuter belt, childcare facilities are open before 8am to allow parents to drop children off on the way to work. And they are still open at 6pm or later to accommodate parents getting back from their jobs.

The childcare providers need to staff up for those hours regardless of how long your child is actually there, so increasingly, the only package they are offering is the Band F package, providing for care of 50 hours or more.

And how does that explain the difference between €959 and €1,400 a month?

The €1,400 figure is the full gross cost before you deduct the subsidy parents are entitled to under the National Childcare Scheme. Once you apply the subsidy, the figure falls to €959. Some parents may just be looking at the top line of their childcare bill.

What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions
