]]><![CDATA[Social welfare, Help-to-Buy, tax changes and childcare costs: Everything we know about Budget 2027 so far]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/16/budget-2027-heres-what-we-know-so-far/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/09/16/budget-2027-heres-what-we-know-so-far/Tue, 06 Oct 2026 10:18:32 +0000Budget 2027, to be presented on October 6th, is due to involve a package of €8.5 billion, with €7 billion in additional spending and €1.65 billion in tax reductions. The cost-of-living issue will be a key focus across the whole package.

Spending – the main issues

While the €7 billion figure is large, an increase of about 6 per cent on this year, much of this money is already effectively allocated to various budgets to keep pace with inflation.

There will be key decisions announced in areas such as health – which is already running well above budget for this year – and education and in what to allocate for a new public sector pay deal. And, of course, in welfare, one of the mainstays of any budget package.

Tax – the main issues

The €1.65 billion package - increased late in the day from €1.5 billion - leaves some for manoeuvre.

Budget 2027: ‘Specific consideration’ for measures to tackle rising heating oil costs

The big move will be a larger than flagged income tax package.

Minister for Finance Simon Harris has suggested that some money could be raised in tax increases, but these will be limited. packet of cigarettes is set to move to €20, though extra tax revenue here will be limited. The bank levy, raising €200 million, is expected to be renewed for another year.

ministers will also have to find money to make some adjustment on inheritance tax and on some new business measures. And to pay the full year cost of the 9 per cent VAT rate for hospitality, announced last year.

Social protection

How much will be allocated to social protection – or welfare – will be a key issue. After some coming and going a general increase of €10 a week has been decided on, the same as the last budget.

The main welfare rates and pensions will be increased by this amount, though the main child benefit rate may stay where it is.

Promises to address child poverty are likely to see additional payments for people on welfare with children – known as child support payments –which are likely to rise by €6 a week. There may also be a further expansion of the Working Family Payment, which is paid to lower-income families on lower earnings.

The much-discussed second tier of child benefit payments which would be paid to all lower income families is not, however, expected to happen this year.

Eligibility for the carers’ allowance is due to be extended, allowing people who have somewhat higher incomes to qualify.

Income tax

An increase in the level at which the higher 40 per cent income tax rate kicks is on the way. The current rate is €44,000 for a single person and €53,000 for a married couple.

An increase of €2,000 had been speculated. However the figure will be €2,500. This means the cut off point for entry to the higher 40 per cent income tax rate rises to €46,500 for a single person and €55,500 for a single earning married couple.

Harris will also indicate that the Government intends to increase the level at which the higher tax rate applies in successive budgets for the rest of its term.

The other big gain from the income tax changes will be from an increase in tax credits. The two main tax credits - the personal and PAYE credit - are both likely to rise by €125. The earned income credit ,which self employed people get instead of the PAYE credit, is expected to increase by the same amount. These would benefit all income tax payers, but give the highest proportional gain to the lower earners.

In broad terms, the standard rate band increase will be worth €500 a year to a single person earning over €46,000. The tax credit rises will add another €250, bringing the total to €750.

The budget will confirm the Government’s decision on an increase in the minimum wage. The Low Pay Commission recommended increasing it by 79 cent per hour, bringing the adult rate from €14.15 to €14.94 per hour from next January and it appears this has been accepted.

There will be a tweak in the entry level for the 3 per cent USC rate to make sure no one on the new minimum wage pays at this level.

A small increase in PRSI, which came into effect at the start of this month, will pull back the total increase in pay packages which workers feel a little when comparing this year with next year.

Income tax change is coming in Budget 2027. Here’s what it means for you

People who get up early were left disappointed by Varadkar. Harris is ready to try again

Energy package

All things energy are hugely politically sensitive and will be central to the package. There will be three key elements – the carbon tax, excise taxes and cash supports to households.

A key focus will be additional supports for those struggling with energy bills through channels such as the fuel allowance scheme or household benefits packages, which help lower-income families meet daily bills.

The Government has resisted the return of energy credits – once-off cash payments to households to lower bills – saying it favoured more targeted, permanent measures.

A big issue will be excise taxes on fuel. These were reduced in two steps earlier this year and the first step to the return of normal rates had been due to take place in November. The Coalition will push the date when this will happen through the winter to March 1st. It will be interesting to see whether Harris hints at further possible extensions if wholesale energy prices remain high.

A Government taskforce has been looking at the area of permanent supports to help households deal with energy costs. As part of this, the budget is likely to have something to say on supports for encouraging retrofitting in older homes and there will also be a scrappage scheme for old boilers, which has already been announced. Grants of €600 are also coming for those installing storage batteries as part of a solar panels investment. This is in addition to grants of up to €1,800 already available for solar PV installations.

The fuel allowances, paid to 470,000 households during the colder months, looks set to increase by €5 a week to €43. There will be an extension of the fuel support scheme for hauliers and farmers. There will also be a fertiliser support package for farmers.

Annual carbon tax increases had been due to be given the go-ahead, as part of a planned series of increases up to 2030. But a big shake-up here is likely and all the increases look set to be put on hold.

The Coalition has indicated that there will be measures to actually reduce the price of home heating oil. The expected route would be to reduce the existing rate of carbon tax on the fuel. The Coalition will also rule out further carbon tax increases on home heating for the rest of its term.

Delaying planned carbon tax increases or reducing existing ones raises questions for spending, as revenue from this tax pays for areas such as SSIA grants for retrofitting – which the Government is trying to speed up – certain fuel-related welfare supports and some climate friendly programmes for farmers..

Disability supports

The Programme for Government commits to a permanent cost-of-disability payment to reflect the higher costs disabled people face in their daily lives. Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary had a public consultation on it earlier this year.

A move is on the cards in the budget, but it will be less than campaigners are looking for. Social Justice Ireland has said a €20-a-week payment would cost €242 million in a year.

A new disability support payment will be announced, but on a lesser scale, involving one lump sum payments of €500, paid next January. There will be a commitment to look at how this support evolves in future.

Tax and Housing

First time buyers will be able to access up to €35,000 towards the deposit on their first home, under the Help-to-Buy scheme, after agreement was reached by party leaders. This increases the limit by €5,000.

There also looks set to be an increase in the rent tax credit, which is worth up to €1,000 per year to a single renter and €2,000 to a couple. A rise of €150 for single people and €300 for a couple if on the cards.

With interest rates on the up, there will be a focus on whether the mortgage tax credit will be renewed. This year it was worth 50 per cent of the increase in mortgage interest paid in 2026 versus 2022, capped at a maximum tax credit of €625.

An improvement in the rent-a-room tax allowances, which allows homeowners to earn up to €14,000 a year from renting out a room to a long-term renter (staying for at least 28 days) is expected.

Inheritance tax

There have been hints from all sides of Government that there would be some move here. Pre-budget documents drawn up by civil servants warned of the high cost of fundamental reform of the tax, such as aligning the tax relief for wider groups inheriting to the levels which currently apply to children.

So it appears there will be modest increases in the three thresholds. The Category A threshold of €400,000 is paid by children inheriting from parents and looks set to rise to €420,000. The Category B threshold of €40,000 applies – generally – to siblings, nieces, nephews, grandchildren and grandparents who get inheritances. The Category C threshold of €20,000, applies in most other cases.

Capital Gains Tax

Senior Ministers have also referred to the possibility of capital gains tax moves, and Harris has said that the 33 per cent rate is “objectively too high”. The budget will announce a 2 per cent cut.

There could be an extension of some CGT reliefs, such as those available to entrepreneurs and a commitment to look at the whole capital tax system, particularly as it relates to investment. The rate of the so-called deemed disposal tax, which put a charge on profits from investments in exchange traded funds every eight years, may be cut.

Savings Scheme

The Minister for Finance is due to announce key details of his savings scheme. The outline shape has already been revealed – it will offer tax-free investment options for households in stocks and shares subject to certain limits. The key question is what these will be. The budget will reveal three key things.

The first is a limit capping what individuals can put in each year - which is €12,000. This looks set to . The second is the total level of a savings fund that will remain free of all taxes. This is €50,000. The third is the level of a new special tax rate that will apply to the assets in the fund above this limit – which is 1 per cent.

Childcare

As part of its cost-of-living package, the Government has promised further help for parents. Its programme promises to cap monthly costs at €200 per child, with progress made over the term of the Coalition. Higher investment to providers under the so-called core funding scheme was already announced to apply from September2026, together with weekly fee caps for parents.

This budget is set to announce a headline reduction of some €1,000 a year for parents of children in full-time care ( 45 hours a week) up to senior infants age. The weekly fees cap will fall to €55.

This will be achieved through an increased subsidy under the National Childcare Scheme - paid to providers and deducted from bills - and a cut in the cap on fees. Earlier reports had suggested these changes could come into effect in January, though the suggestion now is next September. There will also be measures to support the earnings of people working in the sector.

Harris has also hinted at increased tax relief for those minding a child or children in their home. At the moment a minder can earn up to €15,000 tax free per year for minding a maximum of three children – not counting their own. This could rise to €20,000.

Third level

It is expected that there will be an across-the-board €150 cut to student fees. A proposal to cut student fees by €250 a year was reportedly under discussion in late negotiations, but hopes for this had expired by Monday morning. Across the course of the day, however, the idea re-emerged, albeit at a lesser amount, with indications on Monday evening that there would be an extra allocation of around €18 million to deliver the measure.

Some relief appears to be on the cards for families who have more than one child in college through an extension of current discounts which apply to these families.

Culture Giveaway

A plan had emerged to give a €100 voucher 16 year-olds in the Budget to be used for attending arts, music or culture events. A proposal to give such a voucher to 16 and 17 year-olds was part of the Programme for Government. It had appeared that this was going to be subject to further study, but the latest reports say the card will feature in some form in the budget speech.

Business

The Government has made general promises on supporting businesses, but what could happen remains unclear. An extension of research and development relief could be one potential avenue, as well as measures aimed at encouraging investment in domestic industry.

Businesses are also looking for higher spending on training, funded by a surplus in the National Training Fund, but it is not clear is this will happen. It appears now that this is on the cards, with an allocation from the fund for training in AI related areas. A sum of €150 million over three years may be involved.

A fresh rebate scheme on beer kegs is aimed to help rural publicans.

]]><![CDATA[Ardagh weighs selling African glass unit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/06/ardagh-weighs-selling-african-glass-unit/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/06/ardagh-weighs-selling-african-glass-unit/Tue, 06 Oct 2026 10:46:40 +0000Ardagh Group’s new owners are mulling the potential sale of its African glass business as they look to break up the packaging conglomerate to monetise its assets.

Conversations over a possible sale of Ardagh’s Africa business are still largely internal and at an early stage, and there is no guarantee a process will formally kick off, according to people familiar with the matter.

Ardagh declined to comment.

Paul Coulson, who started by taking control of the long-defunct Irish Glass Bottle Company in Ringsend, Dublin, built Ardagh over 25 years into an international glass and metal packaging giant with more than $9 billion (€8 billion) of annual sales, on the back of a series of debt-fuelled deals in so-called junk-bond markets.

That debt became unsustainable when earnings were hit after the Covid-19 pandemic by inflation, soaring interest rates and soft consumer demand on both sides of the Atlantic.

Ardagh looks to sell $3.14bn metal containers business

Late last year, bondholders who were owed $4.2 billion took control of the group with legacy equity holders, including Coulson, being paid $300 million.

Ardagh’s assets are expected to be sold over time rather than through a single transaction, with the various segments probably being marketed to different pools of buyers, the people said, asking not to be identified as they were not authorised to speak publicly.

Ardagh’s glass packaging business also spans Europe and the US, but the African unit is likely to be the first one to be lined up for a sale, the people added.

The African asset is viewed as a high-quality and growth asset, with about 90 per cent of the business coming from South Africa and the rest from Ethiopia, Nigeria and Kenya.

Ardagh was barred from selling its metal-packaging business by a district court in Luxembourg last month, potentially complicating the new owners’ efforts to capitalise on one of the group’s most valuable assets.

The order followed an application from a group of minority creditors who had challenged last year’s restructuring deal. In response, Ardagh had said it was “vigorously challenging the order and has made an application for it to be withdrawn”.

The combined glass packaging businesses in Europe and Africa posted $1.34 billion of revenue in the first six months of 2026, a 7.5 per cent jump year-over-year, according to Ardagh’s most recent report to investors. Adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation stood at $214 million, a 1.4 per cent decline from the same period last year. – Bloomberg

   <description>Nach einem russischen Großangriff auf die Ukraine in der Nacht auf Mittwoch ist die Zahl der Toten weiter gestiegen. Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com regular summaries of news from Poland Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:41:35 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9 https://notesfrompoland.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/cropped-2019-10-29_1838-32x32.png Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com 32 32 Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/08/warsaw-records-eus-highest-employment-rate/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:19:50 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105149

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.

The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.

Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.

The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.

At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).

After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.

Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression.

On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus.

“In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing.

“As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added.

The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members.

Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland.

 

Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise.

This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation.

Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country.

Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027.

“Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. Media reports claim that US President Donald Trump, during a previously unreported meeting earlier this year with Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, suggested that he leave Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and form a new government with the right-wing opposition.

Kosiniak-Kamysz has confirmed that the meeting took place, but has not commented on what was discussed. Meanwhile, Tusk himself has said that, while he wants to “maintain discretion”, the information he received from Kosiniak-Kamysz indicates that Trump was interested in discussing the “internal situation in Poland”.

Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has even more bluntly suggested that the meeting may have served as “an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics”.

Below, we outline how the controversy unfolded, what we know so far, and how senior political figures have commented on the issue.

The context

Poland’s government is a broad coalition that ranges from left to centre right. Although Tusk’s centrist Civic Platform (KO) dominates, it would not have the parliamentary majority necessary to rule if it lost any of its junior coalition partners.

One of those partners is the Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is the most conservative element of the coalition. It has clashed with its partners over issues such as abortion and LGBT+ rights. PSL is led by Kosiniak-Kamysz, who serves as both deputy prime minister and defence minister.

Some elements of the right-wing opposition have suggested that PSL could break with Tusk to form an alternative government, perhaps even with Kosiniak-Kamysz as prime minister. Last year, PSL controversially polled its members on whether they would want to do so. However, PSL and its leader have repeatedly insisted that they remain loyal to Tusk’s coalition.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, the government is in constant conflict with President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition. Nawrocki is also a close ally of Trump, who endorsed him during last year’s presidential election.

By contrast, Tusk and his government have clashed with the Trump administration, though they also seek to maintain close relations with the US as Poland’s most important security partner.

The meeting

The news that Kosiniak-Kamysz had met with Trump in March this year came to light in a rather roundabout way.

On 21 September, Poland’s defence ministry announced that a planned meeting at the Pentagon between Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, planned for 23 September, had been cancelled “at the urgent request of the American side”.

The official reason for the change of plans was Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US at the same time. However, some commentators in Poland claimed that Hegseth had actually cancelled the meeting at the behest of figures close to Nawrocki.

In an effort to debunk those claims, Adam Bielan, a senior PiS figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, claimed that he and Nikodem Rachoń, a presidential advisor, had helped to arrange a meeting earlier this year between Kosiniak-Kamysz and a US figure “much more important than Hegseth”.

Rachoń later confirmed this, but said that the meeting had been secret and he was unable to reveal the identity of the US official. He urged Kosiniak-Kamysz to do so.

 

The defence minister obliged, confirming that the meeting had been with Trump himself and had taken place at the White House on 2 March, alongside a ceremony at which a US army officer, Michael Ollis, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honour for giving his own life to save that of a Polish officer, Karol Cierpica, in Afghanistan.

“I had the opportunity to talk to President Trump for a moment, for which I am very grateful,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz, who noted the role of Nawrocki’s office in arranging the conversation.

What did Trump say to Kosiniak-Kamysz?

Neither Rachoń nor Kosiniak-Kamysz indicated what had been discussed at the meeting. However, last Friday, Dominika Wielowieyska, a leading Polish journalist, claimed that her conversations with various sources, who she did not name, had indicated that Trump used the meeting to encourage Kosiniak-Kamysz to split with Tusk and form a new government with the right-wing opposition.

“Trump suggested to Kosiniak-Kamysz that it would be best if he formed a coalition with the right, and that then they would have 100% support from the United States and the presidential administration, and the door would essentially be open to achieving great success for many Poles,” said Wielowieyska, who writes for Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading liberal daily that is hostile towards Nawrocki and sympathetic towards Tusk.

She added that Kosiniak-Kamysz had immediately shared information about the meeting with the government but that Rachoń had failed to submit a note about it to the foreign ministry, despite that being normal practice and despite a request for a note from foreign minister Radosław Sikorski.

Today, Republika, a right-wing broadcaster with close ties to Nawrocki and the opposition, likewise reported, based on unnamed sources, that, “during the conversation with Kosiniak-Kamysz, there were indications that the Americans were interested in a change of prime minister in Poland”.

What has Poland’s government said?

On Friday, Sikorski took to social media to respond to a claim by Bielan that the Trump-Kosiniak-Kamysz meeting was intended to “unblock” negotiations regarding Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base.

“In the case of such an important conversation, the organiser [Rachoń] had an obligation to prepare a note,” wrote Sikorski, adding that such a document never reached the foreign ministry. “Could that be because the meeting also served as an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics?”

“The conversation was of a confidential nature, and therefore I feel obliged to maintain discretion. It was more about the internal situation in Poland, that’s how I would put it most delicately,” said Tusk.

The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule.

The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020.

However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040.

“This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.”

The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway.

Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two.

The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries.

During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht.

They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September.

On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year.

 

Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives.

Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains.

“For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council.

“Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”.

Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”.

The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced.

The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN.

They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine.

Previously, from 2017 to 2024, Ukraine had banned searches for Polish victims of World War Two on its territory in response to the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist partisan formation that fought against the Soviets but also led the massacre of ethnic Poles.

However, in a major diplomatic breakthrough last year, Ukraine allowed exhumations to resume, including both the Polish soldiers in Lviv as well as victims of the UPA-led massacres, tens of thousands of whom are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves.

The hackers behind a threat to leak Asos customer data duped an employee by posing as a “trusted contact,” the fast-fashion group has said.

An unknown group shocked Asos’ millions of customers on Tuesday when they published a push notification on the online retailer’s app, claiming to have hacked into the company and threatening a data leak.

The incident triggered an immediate sell-off of the London-listed group, as its shares fell more than 13 per cent, casting doubt on the company’s ability to continue its turnaround plan. 

Asos told customers on Thursday morning, in its first announcement since the hack, that it has launched a “detailed investigation” into the incident, apologising for the “uncertainty” caused by the notification.

The fashion group said: “We discovered that an unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain login credentials. 

“Those credentials were then used to access information on certain third-party platforms used by Asos.”

The company said it immediately locked down its platforms to prevent further activity and has referred the incident to “the relevant law enforcement and regulatory authorities”.

The e-commerce firm reassured its customers that the hackers did not access any payment information or passwords, though they did obtain “some personal information, including names and contact details”. 

Asos said: “Once our investigation is complete, we will contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required.

“We know our customers trust us with their information. We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls. Thank you for your patience and for continuing to put your trust in us.”

Asos says app safe to use

Shares in FTSE-250-listed Asos ticked up following the group’s statement, gaining four per cent to 469p.

Asos users were alerted to the hack on Tuesday when a notification appeared on customers’ phones, saying: “Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it.”

Snowflake is a cloud platform used to process data like clothing sizes and body measurements. It also lets users send notifications to clients’ phones.

Snowflake denied that hackers gained access to its systems. A company spokesperson said on Tuesday that it found “no compromise” of its platform.

The notification included a link to a Telegram channel, where a user named ‘Xuanye Group’ said it had obtained customer information which is “safe” on their server and “will not be touched for a designated period”.

“Considering the current situation regarding incident disclosure in the cyber security landscape, you can thank us for our generous clarity regarding this incident,” they added.

British retailers have faced several cyberattacks in recent years. Last year, IT workers at Marks and Spencer were tricked by hackers who gained access to the retailer’s systems.

Shares in Standard Life fell sharply on Thursday as Aberdeen revealed it would sell half of its remaining stake in the company, less than ten years after the messy merger between the two investment firms.

Aberdeen will cut its stake to around 5.2 per cent per cent through a secondary placing, which will value Standard Life’s shares at £8.39 per share and raise £436m.

Standard Life’s shares fell 4.9 per cent to 828p on news of the sale. Aberdeen’s shares rose 0.6 per cent to 236p.

The FTSE 100 group said it would use the money raised from the sale in accordance with its existing cash allocation policy.

This includes “maintaining a strong balance sheet, investing selectively in the business to support sustainable profitable growth, reducing and optimising debt over time, and delivering sustainable returns to shareholders,” the company said.

Evercore Partners is acting as lead financial advisor, while Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Cazenove have been appointed as joint global coordinators.

The messy merger

Aberdeen merged with Standard Life in 2017 in a deal valued at £11bn, but sold the Standard Life business to Phoenix Group for £3.2bn a year later. Phoenix rebranded as Standard Life in March 2026.

Analysts argue Aberdeen’s resurgence has been orchestrated by its acquisition of Interactive Investor, returning it to the FTSE 100 from mid-market exile.

Since its integration into Aberdeen, Interactive Investor has seen steady inflows and has hit multiple record highs.

The platform generated net inflows of £6.8bn in the first half of the year and grew its customer base by 14 per cent to 525,000.

]]> 2464188Maisie Grice Maisie Grice Unlike Brits, America’s wealthiest have lost their sense of duty https://www.cityam.com/unlike-the-brits-americas-wealthiest-have-lost-their-sense-of-duty/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:43:08 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464211

If you are fortunate enough to become wealthy, you have obligations to the society that made that possible. Americans have forgotten that, writes Lewis Liu

I’m dictating a big part of this while driving down Sand Hill Road, perhaps the most concentrated stretch of economic ambition in America. On either side are the venture firms that have funded some of the most consequential companies in modern history. I spend a lot of my life with founders and investors around here. I live exactly one mile away from Sand Hill Road. 

And yet I increasingly think there is one thing Europe still has that America is rapidly losing: a sense of duty.

I don’t mean duty in some nostalgic, aristocratic Downton Abbey sense. I mean something much simpler: the idea that if you are fortunate enough to become wealthy, powerful or influential, you have obligations to the society that made that possible.

A divide between Brits and Americans

When my wife and I decided to move back to America after almost 15 years in London, this was genuinely one of our biggest concerns. We wanted our children to grow up ambitious, competitive and unafraid of risk, all things America is exceptionally good at producing. But we also wanted them to recognise that the country, the community, perhaps even civilisation itself, is bigger than them.

Among many of my European friends, particularly those from old establishment families, that idea is almost instinctive. They talk about wealth and power as things they are stewards of rather than things they simply own and wield.

I remember this during Liz Truss’s spectacularly short premiership. When her government proposed cutting Britain’s top rate of income tax, some of the strongest objections I heard came from friends who would personally benefit. Their response was basically: no, I should pay this. 

Try imagining that conversation in Silicon Valley or Wall Street.

I spend a lot of time mentoring young founders and tech professionals. Many are extraordinarily talented. Some will become exceptionally wealthy. But when I push them on duty, I often get a brutally rational response.

“Lewis, duty is old-fashioned.”

The logic is straightforward. If everyone else is optimising for themselves and I optimise for society, I lose. If I lose, I have less money and less ability to protect myself. So the rational strategy is to win first and worry about society later, if at all.

I recently told one founder that if he was going to devote his life to building something, surely part of that ambition should be making America better.

“Why do I care?” he asked, “America is full of people of different races, backgrounds and values. They have nothing to do with me.”

I said, “fine, but if America breaks, you are in trouble as well.”

His response was revealing: “I can’t control whether America breaks. I can only control what happens to me.”

The old Silicon Valley

To be fair, this is not all of Silicon Valley. Some of the most encouraging conversations I have had recently have been with what I think of as the “old Silicon Valley”, people who made their careers and fortunes in the Google era or even before it.

I often spend time with some pre-eminent post-IPO founders and investors from the previous era, and we have had long discussions on how to bring a sense of civic duty back to Silicon Valley.

What struck me was how naturally they talked about responsibility, community and what successful people owe to the society around them. There was no contradiction, in their minds, between enormous ambition and enormous obligation.

And it made me wonder whether what I am describing is not simply an American problem, but partly a generational one. Somewhere along the way, perhaps the definition of success changed from “what are you responsible for?” to simply “how much have you won?”

That, to me, is the problem.

It is essentially game theory. If you believe you are playing a repeated game over generations, cooperation is rational. You need good schools, safe cities, competent government, infrastructure, social trust and millions of people prosperous enough to buy whatever your company is selling.

But if your time horizon is five or ten years, defection looks rational. Make the money. Sell the company. Move the assets. Buy concierge healthcare, private education, fortressed security.

And once enough people at the top think that way, something dangerous happens.

The system gets worse. The people with the greatest capacity to fix it are the least dependent on it, so they withdraw further. Public institutions weaken. More people feel economically and politically disenfranchised. Trust falls. Anger rises.

This is not a stable equilibrium. It is a ratchet: the more the elite defects, the worse common systems become. The worse those systems become, the larger and angrier the permanent underclass becomes. And eventually, the incentives change again.

At first the instinct is withdrawal: I will simply look after myself. But eventually the instinct becomes control. You find ways to keep people distracted, fragmented, surveilled, dependent or politically weak. Again, there does not need to be a grand conspiracy. Each decision can be individually rational: protect the company, protect the neighbourhood, preserve order, prevent unrest.

But taken together, amoral defection can evolve into something much darker: oppression.

And oppression is not stable either. It produces human suffering, resentment and eventually rupture. Maybe that rupture is political. Maybe it is economic. In the worst case, it becomes violent.

How do we get back on track?

I am not interested in playing armchair historian and predicting some American version of the French Revolution. But logically, a society cannot indefinitely sustain a small group extracting enormous value while a growing majority feels the system no longer works for them, especially if the response to that anger is not reform, but greater control.

So how do we stop the ratchet?

Not by making ambitious Americans less competitive, but by changing what they compete for.

America used to have multiple ways to be elite. A great professor, scientist, judge, diplomat or public servant could hold enormous status and influence without being wildly rich. Now we have collapsed the scoreboard onto one axis: money.

Look at who we put at the top table, who gets invited, listened to and celebrated, including the latest state banquet from Xi Jinping’s visit. We tell ambitious people that the pinnacle of success is becoming extremely rich. Then we act surprised when they optimise accordingly.

So one mechanism is status.

Universities, governments, boards, foundations and the media need to attach prestige and actual influence to service and stewardship again. Not simply philanthropy once you have already made billions, but genuine service.

The second mechanism is more uncomfortable: pay.

America has become so expensive that for many talented graduates, public service feels like financial martyrdom. If you graduate from Harvard or Stanford with loans, a young family and a desire to live anywhere near the institutions where you might serve, a public-sector salary often makes very little economic sense.

Singapore takes a radically different approach, paying senior public servants extremely well precisely because it wants the government to remain a credible elite career.

There is something important in that.

Duty cannot survive on morality alone. It needs an incentive structure.

Europe still has some of the status and tradition. Singapore uses economics. America probably needs some combination of both.

We do not need to make ambition less rewarding. We need to make service more powerful.

Because if the people who benefit most from the system feel no obligation to sustain it, eventually there will not be much left to win.

Leeds United could introduce AI-powered dynamic ticket pricing to increase revenue at the Premier League club, its chairman has said.

Paraag Marathe said the Elland Road club could reward loyal supporters with cheaper prices while pricing tickets for more casual fans at a higher mark-up. 

“There’s probably an opportunity to do it in a way that does increase revenue, but also makes it affordable for your most hardcore fans,” Marathe told sports industry conference Leaders Week London at Stamford Bridge.

“Off the pitch, something that I’ve been thinking about is pricing tickets in the stadium doing dynamic pricing, similar to how the airline industry does it.

“Not just to make to maximise price, but if there’s a way to truly dynamically price based on your supporters – how frequently they go and how much they transact and interact with the club – we can make it more affordable for those folks or certain seats where it’s a little bit more of a hospitality corporate area.”

Leeds United to hike prices?

Dynamic ticket pricing sees the cost of sporting tickets shift depending on demand and closeness to an event. It was deployed, highly controversially, by Fifa during the World Cup across the United States, Canada and Mexico. 

It saw tickets hiked into the thousands of dollars early on before forced cuts to ensure stadiums were full for the quadrennial event.

Organisers of the 2028 European Championships, hosted by the UK and Ireland in two years’ time, have ruled out dynamic ticket pricing for the upcoming tournament. 

The UK government hopes incoming legislation that will enforce a ban on ticket holders selling on secondary markets for a profit will encourage major organisations to price their offerings more competitively. 

“Even right now as we dynamically price, we don’t really use AI. We don’t let it make the decision for us; we just do it in tiers based on what we think,” Leeds United bigwig Marathe, who is also president of 49ers Enterprises and vice chairman of Scottish club Rangers, added.

Following the death of novelist and former political Jeffrey Archer, Eliot Wilson looks back at a complicated life

At the beginning of October 1999, the election for the new post of Mayor of London was only seven months away. Ken Livingstone, left-wing MP for Brent East and the last leader of the Greater London Council before its abolition in 1986, wanted to be Labour’s candidate, while Tony Blair’s New Labour camarilla would have preferred almost anyone else.

The Conservatives saw internal Labour division as a straw and clutched at it. Over the summer of 1999, a frenetic campaign saw novelist Jeffrer Archer and former transport minister Steve Norris battle it out, and Archer won the ballot of party members 71 per cent to 29 per cent.

53 days later it was all over. The News of the World published allegations that Archer had perjured himself in his 1987 libel trial, and he withdrew his nomination.

That Archer had won the candidacy so convincingly in the first place said something profound about him and about the Conservative Party. Jeffrey Archer was a proven and habitual liar. His attitude to financial propriety was casual. Yet when he was summed up, it would be under the rubric of “colourful” or “irrepressible”.

More than any unreliable narrator before Boris Johnson, an element of the Conservative faithful saw his charm and persistence, a Panglossian belief that tomorrow would be better than today, and liked it. He was a lovable rogue whose flaws were offset by this optimism, in a party in which harsh medicine and hard work were often preached.

The son of a conman

Jeffrey Howard Archer was born on 15 April 1940 and grew up in Weston-super-Mare in Somerset. Even as a child, Archer was a fabulist: his mother Lola was a journalist, but he variously described his father William – 64 when Archer was born – as a Royal Engineer, survivor of the fall of Singapore or British consul there (Singapore, a Crown colony, had no consulate), a sergeant in the Somerset Light Infantry and a Distinguished Conduct Medal winner. William Archer was none of these; he was a bigamist and a conman, who died when Jeffrey was 16.

The children of conmen are victims, of course, and often seek solace in the interstices between truth and falsehood: David Cornwell, whose pen name was John le Carré, was an obvious example. In a different way, Archer doubled down on this malign inheritance. He was forever an ambiguous character, capable of misdirection and allowing mistaken inferences to go uncorrected. He won a scholarship to Wellington School in Somerset, an admirable feat, but was relaxed if people assumed he had attended the grander Wellington College in Berkshire.

He left school after his O-levels and drifted through some jobs while inventing others after the fact, almost as if trying on the roles. He did undertake basic training with the Duke of Wellington’s Regiment, then was given a place at Sandhurst but quit without warning after a few months. Archer was also able and determined enough to get through training and spend five months in Brixton as a constable in the Metropolitan Police, but, again, he quickly turned away from the thin blue line.

He spent some time – how much and where has never been verified – in the United States. Later he claimed to have graduated with a BSc from Berkeley, but the university has no record of him.

Having shown genuine promise as an athlete at school, Archer became a public school PE master. He was awarded a fellowship of the International Federation of Physical Culture, and proudly bore the post-nominal letters FIFPC; in fact it was a postal-based body-building club.

Archer went up to Oxford in 1963 to undertake the one-year extramural Diploma of Education. No-one knows how he was accepted, but once there he attached himself inseparably to his host college Brasenose, and spent three years in the city completing his one-year course. He became President of the Oxford University Athletics Club, but more than that he established a claim, shaky but real, to being an “Oxford man”.

Having persuaded the Beatles to participate in an Oxfam fundraiser, Archer then worked as a charity fundraiser. But his vaulting ambition steered him towards politics. The Conservative Party of the mid-1960s was not impenetrable but still required the “wrong” sort of person to work twice as hard for the same result. It was a pressure which exerted a malign effect on the personalities of Edward Heath and Margaret Thatcher, and would leave John Major, later a good friend of Archer, perennially sensitive. Of course CVs and personal background were massaged, but Archer’s embrace of fiction proved to begin years before he wrote his first book.

The political years

In 1967, Archer was elected to the Greater London Council for Havering, at 27, the youngest councillor ever, he said. Actually he was not even the youngest councillor elected that year. When the right-wing Conservative MP for Louth, Sir Cyril Osborne, died in 1969, Archer snatched the nomination and was elected at the December by-election. He claimed to be the youngest MP: he was not, by more than seven years. But in an age before Google and Wikipedia, people were more likely to believe what they were told.

Darker clouds began to gather after his first few years as an MP. First he had to settle a dispute over expenses he had claimed when fundraising for the UN Association. But there was an existential threat on its way, for which he bore little responsibility except ambition. A friend had told him that Aquablast, a Canadian cleaning firm, was on the verge of making enormous sums of money from a new product. Archer borrowed heavily from Anthony Bamford of JCB to invest in the company, which proved to be a scam.

When Aquablast collapsed in 1974, Archer, over-leveraged and in debt to the tune of £500,000 (around £6m today), was facing bankruptcy. If he became bankrupt, he would be disqualified from the House of Commons, so he anticipated the worst by stepping down at the October 1974 election. Now he needed serious money.

Archer was always driven and had implacable self-belief, which came to his rescue. Having exhausted other avenues, he decided to write a best-selling novel. On hearing this, his Oxford athletics friend Adrian Metcalfe challenged him, in an exchange which summed up Archer.

“Jeffrey, you can barely spell, let alone write.”

“That doesn’t matter, I can tell stories.”

Both had a point. Archer wrote Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less, a rags-to-riches tale drawing on his own experience, published first in the US then the UK in 1976. After a slow start, it performed well, then astonishingly well, with the UK paperback selling 3.5m copies. And it heralded the debut of one of the most commercially successful British authors of the age.

Archer was a disciplined writing machine. After as many as 17 drafts, a novel appeared every few years, and the public loved them. Kane and Abel (1979) sold 34m copies worldwide and was adapted for television in 1985. They were undemanding, the writing pedestrian and the dialogue sometimes comically bad. But he wrote to make money, and he understood a formula which appealed to the public in their millions. He was frequently dubbed “the master storyteller”, and that, not the craft of writing or the texture of characterisation, was the key to his success.

With his days in the Commons behind him, Archer became a popular speaker with the Conservative Party membership. In 1985, Margaret Thatcher appointed Norman Tebbit as party chairman, and chose Archer, whom she called “the extrovert’s extrovert”, to be deputy chairman. She understood Archer’s charm as the lovable rogue and knew that it touched parts of the party membership more staid politicians could not reach.

Tebbit was apprehensive; Willie Whitelaw, Thatcher’s irreplaceable deputy, warned her Archer was “an accident waiting to happen”.

It did. In October 1986, The News of the World alleged Archer had paid sex worker Monica Coughlin £2,000 to go abroad; The Daily Star then printed what everyone had been thinking, that Archer himself had paid Coughlin for sex. Archer resigned after 13 months as deputy chairman and promptly sued The Daily Star for libel.

The trial was extraordinary: in his instructions to the jury Mr Justice Caulfield conjured up the testimony of Archer’s wife, Mary: “Remember Mary Archer in the witness-box. Your vision of her probably will never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance?”

The judge moved on to the plaintiff: “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel round about quarter to one on a Tuesday morning after an evening at the Caprice?”

Archer won his suit and £500,000 in damages. Once more the darling of the Tory grassroots, in 1992 he was created Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare. He was tipped for party chairman in the mid-1990s, before the establishment of the London mayoralty offered a final chance of office and power.

But he had lied during the libel trial, having solicited false alibis for himself. In 2000, he was charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice, and was convicted and sentenced to four years in prison. He was released after two years and published three volumes of A Prison Diary, each portentously subtitled after a part of Dante’s Divina Commedia. Archer was seemingly shocked by what he saw and heard, and recorded it with the earnestness of Edward VIII’s “Something should be done to get [South Wales miners] at work again”.

Archer would not have denied being lucky. Living in the Old Rectory in Grantchester, with a Thames-side penthouse full of expensive art where he hosted Krug-and-shepherd’s-pie parties, he was rich from his early 40s until his death on 5 October 2026, aged 86. His final novel, Adam and Eve, was published the same day. He sold 320m books worldwide, and was buttressed by extraordinarily indulgent family and friends.

Many of his social circle attest to an intense, almost guileless charm, and there was something winning about his refusal to accept defeat. One of his oldest friends, critic Sheridan Morley, explained: “The best way to think about Jeffrey is to treat him as if he comes from another planet… he thinks [it] is going to be all right in the end.”

He was lucky in his spouse of 60 years, distinguished (and “fragrant”) scientist Dr Mary Archer. She was loyal and discreet, and could only bring herself to approach his relentless mendacity by admitting he had “a gift for inaccurate précis”.

It was not “inaccurate précis”. Archer had since his youth gone well beyond the bounds of setting facts in the best possible light and perhaps helping their lustre a little. Some of the things he claimed simply were not, could not have been true, but he was more than willing to invent, amend or delete when it was to his advantage. In Morley’s phrase, it was “all right in the end”, at least for him.

A “master storyteller” and well-connected multi-millionaire, Archer was blessed by commercial appeal and a fearsome work ethic. Many found him personally kind and delighted in his hospitality. As a behemoth of books, he was unstoppable, despite a pedestrian prose style. But he was also a liar, tried and tested. He wrote fiction for a living as well as let it shape his personality. Each aspect has its cheerleaders, but we all of us have to judge for ourselves. 

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian

The director of Ian Charleson’s 1989 National Theatre Hamlet production speaks to City AM about a long career in showbusiness, and how often national treasures have a dark side.

Richard Eyre has worked as a director of stage and film since the 1960s, with his most famous movies including Iris and Notes On A Scandal.

He has directed London theatre since the 1960s and in 1989 directed Ian Charleson when he was artistic director of the National Theatre. In Andrew Scott’s Elsinore, Richard Eyre is portrayed by Johnny Flynn. The movie follows the life of the actor Ian Charleson who passed away from AIDS seven weeks after playing the role of Hamlet at the National Theatre in 1989.

The topic of the NHS is a big one throughout Elsinore as the men with AIDS receive their treatment, and Eyre has often been interested in telling stories to do with health, particularly about old age, which was the subject of a recent film of his.

For Richard Eyre, who also directed the movies Stage Beauty, The Other Man and Allelujah, the state of our NHS makes for rich drama. The number of over-60s around the world will almost double from 2015 to 2050, according to the latest data from the World Health Organisation. Amid this staggering rise, the NHS is facing constant calls for further funding, and health inequality widened significantly under the pandemic.

Eyre isn’t alone in thinking so: last year’s BAFTA winning Jodie Comer drama Help proved how stimulating drama about the underfunding of the NHS can be. And now, the lives of those impacted by the challenges faced by the NHS are explored in Richard Eyre’s new film, Allelujah, adapted from the Alan Bennett play. Premiering this Sunday 9 October at the BFI London Film Festival at the Royal Festival Hall, and with further screenings next week, the picture is an emotional plea for more action to be taken by the government.

It’s about old people – a group in which I don’t, of course, include myself

Richard Eyre, who soon turns 80, jokes about his own years

“It’s about old age and care of old people – which is a group in which I don’t, of course, include myself,” jokes 79-year-old Richard Eyre down Zoom. Eyre, the former artistic director of the National Theatre, most notably directed Notes On A Scandal starring Judi Dench, who also stars in Allelujah, as well as Iris, a feature about novelist Iris Murdoch, who suffered from dementia. The topic of ageing is familiar and recurring in Eyre’s work.

“Obviously the issue of old age is of material interest to me,” he says. “What are we supposed to do with the extra years?” In Allelujah, set in an underfunded hospital in Yorkshire that’s fighting for survival, we experience the ways ageing affects people of every age: we meet angry middle-aged people thirsty for their inheritance, and emotionally detached younger people who have paper thin relationships with their elders. But the message is clear: as more of us live longer, the ‘issue’ of what it means to be older in an ageing society isn’t going away.

“The government who have underwritten the NHS have not really taken this into consideration,” according to Eyre. “The NHS is constantly under pressure and we don’t seem to be getting a public understanding of how to deal with the ‘problem’ with old age. What do we do with old age, how do you provide for the frail and vulnerable. They’re always at the end of the list. if you look at provision for care homes, it’s shocking. They’re desperately under funded.”

Alongside Dench, Allelujah stars Russell Tovey, and Jennifer Saunders in a rare straight role. In the hospital, scenes depict residents singing renditions of the classics around the piano, bringing moments of cheer. But crucially for Eyre, there are more pressing topics than joy: “I would like to be able to paint a picture of joyous old age but often the body militates against it.”

There are countless stories to tell around ageing which have still not been told. “There is so much bias now towards the young,” he says, “towards feeding a younger audience.” It’s an approach the Devon-born director believes might be counterproductive: “I think statistically you could demonstrate that a much higher proportion of older people watch television because at a certain age you don’t watch television at all. I certainly didn’t watch much television in my twenties.”

Judi Dench is as gripping as you’d ever hope in her role as a savvy resident who ends up with a crucial sleuthing role in the drama, revealing murky goings on at the hospital. Like the residents of the fictional care home, Dench, too, is ageing, and at 88, Eyre’s feeling is that these days she’s happier playing smaller roles. The Bond veteran is “reluctant to take on that responsibility and be on set every,” he says, but was very happy to be involved with Allelujah. “She was working with a lot of people that she knew and loved her.”

Some star actors would be very hard to get together – they might be all fighting over their individual territory

Richard Eyre, who’s known for all-star British casts in his films

Eyre and Dench first met in the mid-to-late sixties when he was in his mid-twenties. “We remained friends ever since,” he says, singing her praises: “She’s a very rare person in that she’s everything that people say she is. And usually people who are described as national treasures and are infinitely hugely talented, hugely generous, there’s a dark side. Well there isn’t. What you see is what she gives. And that’s a very very intelligent, witty and brilliant person and a very loyal friend.”

What might Dench and Eyre discuss when the camera stops rolling? “I guess I can just call her up and say, ‘Do you fancy being in this film, it’s not a very large part but I think you’d enjoy it?’” Eyre says of their friendship. “She doesn’t like a lot of discussion about the character and how to approach it, she likes to rely on instinct and her intelligence. She’ll ask questions that are very direct and specific and she just wants an answer to that question. She doesn’t want a whole series of explanations around the character, she’s always very precise and very specific and being specific is what makes for good performances.”

Despite the roll-call of British talent present in Allelujah, Eyre insists he hires actors “entirely on the basis of who is best for the part.” But there’s another benefit to having an ensemble of talent UK audiences are familiar with: it’s likely 50% of the actors on a UK film have worked together before because our acting scene is centralised in London unlike in the States, where theatre is east coast and film and TV is west. The chemistry that actors develop over a lifetime of working together is an easy win for UK productions, and Eyre says of casting A-Listers: “I’m sure there are gatherings of star actors who would be very hard to get together because they might be all fighting over their individual territory, but all these people are people are used to working as a company.”

I have a 50% success rate with my projects. That’s enough for me to keep going

Richard Eyre on his relationship with critics

There’s another benefit to casting star names: crafting that element of surprise. Saunders’ nurse character has a dark side revealed later in the drama, and admittedly, it’s odd seeing the Ab Fab legend playing a stern character. “I like the fact that people might approach this film thinking, ‘Oh it’s Jennifer Saunders from Ab Fab,’” says Eyre. “I enjoy the fact that people might have different expectations and that those expectations will not be realised when they see she is just a first class actor.” Next year, as Eyre enters his eighties, he’s keen to keep telling stories about people in their older years.

He has particular interest in stories around voluntary euthanasia, “to cite a not very popular subject,” and dementia, “because my mother had Alzheimer’s,” but having just written his first London play, The Snail House at the Hampstead Theatre, he also has plans for more writing. “I was obviously disappointed that it wasn’t better received by the press and maybe they had excessively high expectations of this particular first time writer,” he says – but he’ll keep going. The process of beginning to write at 79 – and working in general – “keeps the blood flowing and the heart rate up.”

“If you were put off by critics then we’d have all given up a long time ago,” he says. “If everything you do gets the thumbs down then you’d be a fool or insane not to take notice of it, but I guess I have a good 50% success rate with my projects. So that’s enough for me to keep going and have an appetite for what’s to come.”

Despite the rise of stories depicting the epidemic, the horrors of AIDS are still underrepresented in film and TV. Russell T Davies’ It’s A Sin brought freshness by focusing on fleeting moments of joy, and Simon Stone’s Elsinore borrows from that playbook with this magnificent story that follows one victim’s remarkable life.

Andrew Scott will now be celebrated not for his LGBTQ storytelling in All Of Us Strangers, but for Elsinore, his focused, magnetic account of the true tale of Ian Charleson, the actor who played Hamlet at the National Theatre in 1989, seven weeks before he passed away from the disease.

Elsinore film: I was shallow breathing throughout

Scott, who produces and stars, is devastatingly good as the man who would rather “die of Hamlet than of AIDS,” delivering agonisingly realistic blow-by-blow accounts of the pain Charleson was experiencing. 

In one agonising scene, he rocks back and forth while having a seizure that feels grippingly lifelike: Scott’s impression of the frenzied Charleson in hospital haunts long after the credits; but his remarkably truthful performance brings lightness too, conveying Charleson’s rom-com warmth as well as his coyness.

It is a flatly astonishing story. Beresford’s script follows Charleson’s true, remarkable tale, as the actor prepares to take on the sword-bearing Prince of Denmark in spite of regular sicknesses that cause him to be bed bound in the weeks leading to opening night. 

Though Elsinore, named after the fictitious castle in Hamlet, never gets waylaid by misery. There are plenty of laughs and heart-warming cameos. “You will perform,” Chaleston insists to one young Aids victim, played by Heartstopper’s Joe Locke, and we’re treated to a dozen patients delivering a choreographed musical number from the hospital ward. 

Elsinore opens London Film Festival

There are hedonistic dinner parties; immersive depictions of cruising; and we’re plunged into rehearsals for Hamlet, camerawork bringing us within dripping distance of Scott’s perspiring pores, and then there is the National Theatre: dour, soggy shots around the Southbank cast the venue as a second, quiet lead.

An impeccable supporting cast includes Olivia Colman as Charleson’s no-nonsense doctor and LGBTQ ally, credited with extending the lives of thousands of men, and Billie Piper fizzes with tenderness, offering great comic timing as best friend Monica. 

Scott, folded over and retching off stage after delivering the Prince’s lines, is just wretched, compelling viewing. You feel so desperately for all these men, and Elsinore draws you closer than ever to these subjects. At the press screening during the London Film Festival, running until 17 October, a rare round of applause from tight-lipped critics.

Almost 20,000 men died of AIDS in the UK alone before effective treatment came in in the mid-1990s. While early depictions of the epidemic like The Normal Heart, which premiered at the Royal Court in 1986, can feel didactic by today’s standards, Andrew Scott is surely due an Oscar for the agonising detail examined in Elsinore, which sketches out a fresh rulebook for a new era of LGBTQ storytelling.

Elsinore is in UK cinemas from January 29

Big Four giant Deloitte has been fined £11m for failing to raise concerns about fraud in its statutory audits of the transport business, the Go-Ahead Group (GAG), which operates multiple train services across the UK.

The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) said on Thursday the fine, which was discounted to £6.05m for early admission and co-operation, related to the Big Four giant’s audit of the transport firm between the 2016 and 2020 financial years.

GAG, a major transport group, provides rail and bus services across the country, and from 2016 to 2020, the group was listed on the London Stock Exchange. The group is London’s largest bus operator, running roughly a quarter of the capital’s buses across 17 depots on behalf of Transport for London (TfL), including the Elizabeth Line.

The breaches relate to three of GAG’s subsidiaries that operated passenger rail services: London and South Eastern Railway Ltd (LSER), London and Birmingham Railway Ltd (LM), and Go-Ahead Bayern GmbH (GABY). The findings on Deloitte’s failure to apply “professional scepticism” regarding three subsidiaries. The regulator found that, in each case, Deloitte accepted management’s explanations without sufficient challenge.

The FRC said Deloitte, across all three subsidiaries, failed to recognise that it had wrongfully retained over £30m in taxpayer funds by keeping overpayments to the Department for Transport (DfT), and it failed to address the transport group’s concerns.

The Big Four firm also received a severe reprimand alongside the fine and an order to prepare a report for Deloitte’s FRC firm supervisor explaining why these failures happened. The regulator said Deloitte must pay the full costs of the FRC’s investigation.

“These breaches show a highly concerning pattern of failure by Deloitte to apply sufficient scrutiny to decisions and actions by GAG which were clearly questionable. The fact that some of those decisions and actions put very large amounts of UK taxpayers’ money at risk is particularly troubling, and this is reflected in the high level of financial sanction imposed,” said Penrose Foss, executive counsel and executive director of investigations and enforcement.

Commenting on the fine, a spokesperson from Deloitte UK said: “We regret that aspects of our audit work did not meet the standards expected and have learned from this matter. We are committed to continuous improvement and the delivery of high quality audits.”

Regulator drops Joules probe

Separately, the regulator also announced on Thursday that it closed its probe into Deloitte over its audit of former listed lifestyle brand Joules Group. 

The FRC launched the investigation in May 2023 after Joules collapsed into administration in late 2022, reviewing the audit for the year ended 30 May 2021. 

The British fashion retailer, founded by Tom Joule, collapsed into administration on 16 November 2022. A month later, retail giant Next partnered with founder Tom Joule to acquire the business out of administration in a £34m to £41m deal.

After a “review of the evidence and all relevant factors” from Deloitte’s audit of the business, the FRC closed its investigation into the Big Four giant without taking any enforcement action.
